Since both the aspect (*ākāra*) and the perceived object (*ālambana*) are mere conceptual constructions (*parikalpita*), this interpretation is correct; other interpretations are incorrect."
The Master Bi said: "This refers to those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) and those who have attained liberation through the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

The underlying meaning is that the name "Supreme Fruit" (*viśeṣaphala*) is established in contrast to the Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment and the liberated ones of the Two Vehicles; for both the stage of Equal Enlightenment and the Two Vehicles are, in relation to the Buddha, [inferior].

The Secret [Teaching] says: "That which is called 'Equal Enlightenment' is spoken of in terms of a long duration. The intended meaning is this: in a single moment, the two wisdoms are equal to the Buddha.
Nevertheless, although they are equal to the Buddha in a single moment, from the perspective of a long duration, they do not reach the level of the Buddha.
This is because the Buddha has already attained the Way, having perhaps passed through many kalpas; thus, when compared to that long duration, the Bodhisattva does not [attain it].
It is called "Victorious Bodhi. Because it has been a long time since the Buddha attained enlightenment, it is called "Long Duration.

Regarding the secret [teaching] that says, "From the Path of Uninterrupted [Activity] to Liberation," the intended meaning is as follows: It is reckoned that one should attain liberation by severing the obstacles in the Path of Uninterrupted Activity and realize the fruit;
thus, one is immediately named a Buddha. Why, then, is it said here that they "simultaneously sever a single obstacle"? The answer is: based on the actual Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
It has already been severed. This is the Buddha. From the perspective of being free from obstructions, it is also called "severing obstructions";

in reality, they have already been severed. Question: When the two supreme fruits are realized, both obstructions are eliminated simultaneously. Why, then, is it said that only one obstruction is severed? Answer:

Although there are many types of obstructions, because they are equally obstructions and because they equally obstruct the single fruit of Buddhahood, they are collectively referred to as "one obstruction. It is not for [other reasons].
To say "a single obstruction" and that there is nothing further refers to the interpretation of the Tripiṭaka.
To say "threefold reflection" refers to the three gates of liberation, namely emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

The Secret [Teaching] says: "Manifesting as Perfect Enlightenment" refers to the Omniscient One. This means the Wisdom of the Essential Nature (*svābhāvika-jñāna*). It asks: Why is it called "Omniscience"?
Because True Suchness (*tathatā*) pervades all things, the wisdom of True Suchness realized through the severance of delusions is also termed "Omniscience.
Regarding the phrase "thoroughly and skillfully penetrating this Wisdom of the Characteristics of the Path," this explains the function of the aforementioned Correct Wisdom.

This is so. "Manifest" (*pratyakṣa*) refers to direct perception; "equal" (*sama*) means it includes all other distinct categories of present phenomena. The wisdom that is able to fully comprehend these is called the "wisdom of all aspects" (*sarvākārajñatā*).

This implies that it is associated with the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). "Manifest" means the present; "equal" means it encompasses all various types of present phenomena; because this wisdom can thoroughly understand them all, it is named the wisdom of all aspects.
Alternatively, it may be understood as referring to both the past and the future, because wisdom is capable of comprehending them.
Regarding the statement, "All afflictions (*kleśa*) are able to continue rebirth," the intended meaning is as follows: there are two interpretations. First, this applies to all afflictions;
although they may manifest collectively later on, there are still those that do not give rise to karma. Although they do not give rise to karma, [they still have the capacity to continue rebirth].
Regarding the assistance rendered from afar to those who are identical, this generally refers to not taking up seeds; however, it may also be understood as taking them up.

According to the father’s explicit statement that "not taking up" is the primary [condition], this refers to the arising of a distinct body. A "distinct body" refers to the present *ātmabhāva* (personal existence), which is considered "distinct" in relation to the body of the future birth;
this principle may be applied analogously through successive stages.
The Secret Commentary states: "Regarding the claim that what is designated as the 'entire realm' (kṛtsnadhātu) is based on its arising and manifestation, the intended meaning is this:

one takes only that which moistens manifest activity (saṃmukhībhāva) to be the entire realm. Although pride (māna) and other afflictions may manifest, if they do not moisten the gateway to rebirth, they are not included.
Furthermore, it is doubted whether the father’s assistance in karma—which, though not moistening [rebirth], nevertheless manifests—should also be called the entire realm."
The Master said: "A 'partial severance' refers to the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*).

There is a partial obstruction to the contemplation of reality that prevents sentient beings from attaining the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*); since these have now been suppressed, it is called 'partial.

That 'partial nirvāṇa' has the meaning of tranquility (*śānti*), as it resembles the tranquility of the *tathatā* (suchness) of the Buddha-dharma. As for the phrase 'not definitive,' it means that the desire to sever them is not yet definitive."
Mi said: "If it is argued that there is no fault because the thesis statement is definitely not non-existent according to the rules of formal logic (*nyāya*), the intended meaning is this:

if the thesis states that [the object] truly exists, then one would incur the fault of using anger and so forth, or a jar and so forth, as examples. Why? Because these are fallacious (*sādṛśya*). Now, the thesis states that they are not..."

There is none; thus, the aforementioned fault does not apply. Why is this? Because although things such as jars and mental states such as anger are "semblances," they are not devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

[The opponent] says: "The reason (*hetu*) also commits the fault of being definitively contradictory (*viruddha*). The intention here is that it establishes a definitive contradiction with the reason provided by the other party.

Regarding the fallacy of contradiction (*viruddha*): while the subject (*dharmin*) remains unchanged as previously stated, the thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are all modified.
Each of these may be understood by comparing them to the preceding [correct] formulation.
The Master said: "From 'formless' up to 'bodiless,' these refer to the mental sphere (*manāyatana*) and all states of mind.

Because they are not material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) and cannot be seen, they are called 'bodiless. This means that within the physical sense organs (*rūpendriya*), they are said to dwell in a cavern."
The Secret [Commentary] says: "How could one who possesses a spear and lance [be so]"? The intended meaning is that this reveals a contradiction. How is it contradictory? The answer is:
suppose there is a person carrying a spear while walking, and someone asks, "What is this for? He replies, "This spear is hard and sturdy."

Yet he was able to subdue bandits; his sword clanged without striking anyone, and no creature could withstand him. Furthermore, he walked while brandishing a spear—where "spear" (shao) refers to a commemorative stele.
If someone were to ask, "What is this object for? he would answer as before. Is it not the case that his earlier and later statements contradict one another?

The *Biji* (Secret Commentary) states: "To say that 'non-existence' (*wu*) means there is neither a partial absence nor a total absence of mental factors" means that when there is a total absence of mental factors, it is called "absence of [mental] objects," and when there is a partial absence of mental factors, it is also called "absence of [mental] objects.

However, because there are only three types of non-existence and not many, it is termed "partial absence," just as a small amount of water is also called "no water. When the treatise says "the Master of the Treatise also implies this," the meaning is that [he refers to] the three.
The masters all possess [these qualities]. Now, in composing this treatise, I have done so intentionally; I shall not cite them at length, as they are already implicitly revealed.

Regarding the question, "In the thirty verses, how many are subsumed within each [of the three parts]? the intention is to say: "If you were to establish [the doctrine] by means of these three parts..."

Regarding the Proponents of Consciousness-Only (*Vijñānavādin*): I have not yet ascertained how many verses from the *Thirty Verses* each of the three parts—namely, the "seeing" (*darśana*) and so forth—are subsumed within.

As for the phrase "how could there be": this means, "What kind of meaning does 'there being' (*asti*) express? Regarding the statement "How could there be such a principle?": what kind of logical principle could possibly exist [in that case]?
Bimi said: "Regarding the *Saṃgraha* establishing its tenfold excellence (*viśeṣa*), it is as complete as the categories of dharmas.
Bimi said: "As for these two treatises reaching the 'object, practice, and fruit' (*ālambana-pratipatti-phala*), the meaning is that this refers to the main body of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*."

The three—object, practice, and fruit—are clarified. Now, regarding this *Vijñaptimātratā* (Consciousness-Only), it likewise follows that fundamental doctrine in clarifying these three: object, practice, and fruit; thus, it constitutes the primary and skillful core of the system.
As for the secret [instruction], it says:

"Furthermore, what is called 'fundamental wisdom' (*mūla-jñāna*) is termed 'divine' (*deva*) upon reaching the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*). The intent of this is that within the Path of Vision there is non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*).

Wisdom (*jñāna*). Taking suchness as its object is the dharma; when the mind and its object are in profound accord, this is called wisdom (*jñāna*) at the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).

The Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) is called "spiritual power" (*ṛddhi*). Because one proceeds from the Path of Preparation (*prayogamārga*) to the Path of Seeing, it is termed the "conjunction of wisdom. Spiritual power is the functional application of wisdom;
upon reaching the Path of Seeing, the functional application of wisdom gradually increases.
The *Bimi* (Secret) states: According to that scripture, at the four hundred and ninety-eighth [fascicle], it says, "even unto what is called 'the mundane' (*yemian*).

The intent is this: based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Great *Pāramitā* is explained as being "mundane. This refers to the question posed by Śāriputra, which the *Bimi* school has cited here;
therefore, each point must be explained individually. First, "that which is mundane" refers to that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
The essence of the six pāramitās is as follows: "Creating the world" refers to the practice and cultivation of the six perfections.
"Arising from the world" refers to cultivating the six perfections by means of having a physical body. "Equal to the world" refers to cultivating the six perfections for the sake of future fruits.

"Proceeding from the world" refers to cultivating the six perfections starting from one's own person. "Belonging to the world" refers to these impure (sāsrava) mental states of the six perfections which have not yet—
Because it transcends the world, it is called "belonging to. To rely on the mundane means to practice by depending upon these six perfections.
To call it "mundane" is simply to name it as such; the commentary states: "To call it 'mundane' is merely a term of address."

Bimi said: "That which transcends the world refers to the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) and so forth that are free from outflows (anāsrava). This can also be explained by relying on the eight case-inflections (aṣṭau vibhaktayaḥ), and its meaning is thus understandable.
Bimi said: "Regarding the term 'transcending the world,' 'name' (nāman) refers precisely to the eight types of vocal intonation."
Miji said: "The title of the fascicle is also erroneous; it refers to the *Prajñāpāramitā* in four hundred and ninety-eight fascicles.
The commentary states that the claim of 'five hundred fascicles' is an error."
The Master Bi said: "As for the statement in various *Huajing* (Flower Sūtras) that 'one comes to enter this dwelling,' the intended meaning is this:

since the Dharma-purity has already resided within the triple world (*tridhātu*), how could it be said again that one 'comes to enter' this dwelling? It is merely spoken with reference to the subsequent slight increase in karmic fruit."
This case is also like that.

Bi said: "Regarding the statement 'even existence ultimately does not exist,' the intended question is as follows: For instance, take the essence of my own dharma; it is something that is without any object of attachment."

If that which is perceived after the perception has ceased were non-existent, how could the holy teachings take non-existence as their basis? For non-existence takes the perceived characteristics (*nimitta*) as its basis, because one calculates [them] as self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*).
Vasubandhu says: "That which is called 'attachment' in worldly discourse applies to all"—the meaning is that this refers to both the mundane outflows (*āsrava*) and the holy teachings.
Regarding Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles, that portion of their afflicted mental states which manifests as a self and phenomena lacks a basis;
this is because all afflicted minds and mental factors are attachments. As for the uncontaminated [states] of Bodhisattvas and so forth, as well as those manifested by Buddhas—
All are merely strong conceptual designations (*prajñapti*). That is to say, the meaning [of "self" and "dharmas"] depends upon their substance.

Within the uncontaminated minds (*anāsrava-citta*) of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, there appears the semblance of a principle that maintains a single, permanent meaning; this is called the existence of self and dharmas. All sentient beings likewise possess such semblances of conceptual designations.

The Secret Commentary states: "If the uncontaminated mind (*anāsrava-citta*) reaches the point where it is said to be 'resembling' based on self-realization (*svasaṃvitti*)," the intended meaning is as follows:

Master Sthiramati holds that both parts [the object-aspect and the subject-aspect] are entirely the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). This was stated in reference to the object-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and subject-aspect (*darśanabhāga*) of sentient beings.

Now, however, this is stated in reference to the uncontaminated self-realization aspect. Question: Why is it not stated in reference to the two parts of the object-aspect and subject-aspect? Answer: Because the uncontaminated mind lacks the object-aspect and subject-aspect.

This refers to the "divisions. To say that there is a distinction between the "transforming subject" (the grasper) and the "transformed object" (the grasped) means that the self-verifying division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) is the transforming subject, while the self (*ātman*) and dharmas are the transformed objects.

Thus, one should understand that when the term "transformation" is mentioned, it is not known to refer solely to the establishment of the distinction between the seeing and image divisions (*darśana-bhāga* and *nimitta-bhāga*).

The Secret [Commentary] says: "Furthermore, speaking according to the primary meaning" means that one adopts the first interpretation from among the two preceding explanations. The Secret [Commentary] says:
"'The post-attainment state of mutual perception is not what my doctrine relies upon'" means that if one were to take the self and phenomena as the basis for self-realization...
Regarding that which is transformed by the divisions [of consciousness]: the "seeing" and "image" portions cannot serve as the basis for the self and dharmas.

Therefore, one should know that these words only explain the image and seeing portions as being transformations of consciousness; they do not state that this self and these dharmas are themselves the transformations of consciousness.
Rather, they are merely established based upon the image and seeing portions as something resembling them.

The Secret Commentary says: "Regarding the point that this [definition] would overextend to the seventh consciousness, the intention is as follows: if one were to state it specifically that 'that which cognizes an object is called the consciousness that cognizes objects,' this would overextend to the seventh consciousness.
Why? Because the seventh consciousness also takes the eighth consciousness as its object by way of specific cognition."
It should also be called the "consciousness that cognizes objects.
[The Master] Mi said: "Even though there are two, three, or up to eight, there is no distinction among them. This means that although the first truth is indeed the second conventional truth.

If one considers them according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there are eight distinctions regarding their existence. If one considers them according to the first [level of] ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) for the noble ones (*ārya*), there are likewise eight distinctions.

Why? Because the ultimate is superior to the conventional. Regarding the secret synthesis into two sections, from the passage in the treatise beginning with "it is said" up to "also exists as the ultimate," [the text proceeds].
The text is divided into two sections. The first section, from "The treatise says" up to "the object exists as a reality," provides a specific explanation of the three phrases.
The second section, from "Having established what the deluded conceive" up to "also exists as the ultimate truth," provides a general explanation of the three phrases in relation to the preceding.
This division of the treatise into two sections is termed the "Two-Section Arrangement."
The Secret [Commentary] states: "There is a principle that the function of reaching an object must depend upon a substantially real essence. The meaning is this:

a non-existent dharma cannot produce cognition by way of its essential nature (*svabhāva*). If someone were to conceive of a non-existent dharma and claim that such a non-existent dharma can produce cognition, it would be speaking in terms of an essential nature.

In fact, non-existent phenomena cannot produce understanding. Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* is cited as stating: "It is only said that the functioning of conditions must depend on phenomena with real substantial entities;

it is not said that phenomena without substantial entities can produce understanding. Thus, we know that a non-existent phenomenon cannot be called a "normative standard" (*pramāṇa*), because it cannot give rise to the understanding of things.
The Secret [Commentary] says: "To answer based on the essence of the arising consciousness" refers to the meaning of the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*) and other texts.

This means that if the essence of the arising consciousness must have a substantial dharma as its condition (*pratyaya*), then even if there were no substantial dharma for the production of mental application and understanding (*ākāra-prajñapti*), such application and understanding could still arise with that [non-substantiality] as their condition.

For example, because the self (*ātman*) does not exist, the very statement "the self does not exist" gives rise to mental application and understanding; "mental application and understanding" refers to—
This is the function of consciousness.

This refers to the various characteristics; it does not adopt the restricted name [of the fruit] as it is conferred by the terminology.

This refers to the knowledge of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*). The intended meaning is that the path of preparation and the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) are collectively termed "approaching" (*pratipannaka*).
Regarding the phrase "the second, prior to the addition": the intention is that, according to the second interpretation, there are two kinds of approaching;
the second clause is indeterminate, as it pertains to the first interpretation prior to the addition.
The Secret Commentary states: "Regarding the phrase 'because there are differences up to the stage of being directed toward the first [fruit],' the intended meaning is as follows:

this refers to the stage of being directed toward the first fruit (*prathamaphalapratipannaka*), which also includes two types—those who leap over (*vyutkrāntaka*) and those who follow the sequence (*anupūrvaka*). Both receive indeterminate names.

As for those who follow the sequence, from the time they have abandoned the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) up until the fifteenth moment of mind, they are collectively termed 'directed toward. If they reach the sixteenth moment of mind, they are then [the fruit itself]."
Because it is subsumed under the fruit, this is the sequential candidate (*anupūrvaka-pratipannaka*).

As for the leap-over candidate (*vyutkrāntaka-pratipannaka*), this refers to a person of sharp faculties who, having previously suppressed the afflictions through supramundane paths by cultivating three or four stages, is still prior to the fifteenth moment of the path of seeing;

they are also called a candidate. Although they have abandoned [the afflictions of] three or four stages of cultivation, they are still called a candidate for the first fruit (*prathamaphala-pratipannaka*). Upon reaching the sixteenth moment of mind...
This is subsumed under the first fruit itself. Question: What is the difference between one who transcends toward the first fruit and one who proceeds gradually toward the second fruit?
Answer: This one who transcends toward the first fruit, prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), has previously suppressed the cultivation of three or four categories [of afflictions].

Upon reaching the fifteenth moment of mind within the path of seeing, these are abandoned simultaneously with the afflictions of the path of seeing; thus, they are established as being directed toward the first fruit. As for the gradual candidate:

After the fruit has been attained, from the point when five categories [of afflictions] have been abandoned, one is then established in the second *pratipannaka* (candidate); this refers to a distinction in their attainment. Question:
What is the difference between the first *abhisamayapratipannaka* (candidate for the direct realization) and the second *abhisamayapratipannaka*? Answer:

Although both are of a single type of transcendence (*abhisamaya*), it is because the second category first suppresses [the afflictions] without depending on [the previous fruit] that there is a distinction. If one possesses sharp faculties, they immediately cultivate...

Regarding the five stages (*pañca-varga*), the second candidate (*dvitīya-pratipannaka*) is established; from the time one has abandoned the third and fourth categories of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) up until the fifteenth moment of mind, the first candidate (*prathama-pratipannaka*) is established.
Although this interpretation exists, doubts and obstructions still remain: why is there a distinction between two candidates for a single type of person who transcends [the stages]?
Could it be that a person who transcends as a first candidate, having abandoned the first three or four categories of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation, does not [attain the fruit]?
This is called the second *pratipannaka* (candidate for the next fruit). Must one necessarily abandon five categories [of afflictions] to be designated as the second *pratipannaka*? Answer:

Although this principle exists, because the fundamental minds of application (*prayoga-citta*) differ, there is a distinction in their destinations. What fault is there in establishing two candidates?

Although this interpretation exists, if the logic and scriptural teaching are not clear, then by this one knows that the lower abandonment is not accepted. The second interpretation is simply... [text fragment].
This is the second interpretation.

Bi says: "The second can be reconciled" means that it is established based on the distinction between whether the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) have been severed or not.

Regarding the first fruit-candidate (*pratipannaka*), the second [fruit] is severed; thus, "the second can be reconciled" means that if one relies on this explanation, then the second interpretation is indeed consistent. If...

In the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the principles and teachings are clear; however, those whose modes of practice (*ākāra*) are entirely distinct do not reach the level of the aforementioned understanding.

Question: Why is the third candidate (*pratipannaka*) not mentioned? Even though there are those who proceed through the stages sequentially or by leaping over them. Answer: It is not mentioned because they are few.
According to the Yǎnbì school, they also permit this explanation. Yǎnbì says:
"Regarding 'venerating, accumulating, producing, and the causes,' the meaning is as follows: 'venerating' (chóng) means lofty veneration; it carries the sense of piling up or accumulation."

The Secret [Commentary] says: "That which is capable of producing and growing those functions" means that these sense bases (indriya) are able to produce the functions of those minds and mental factors (citta-caitta).
If those bases were absent, the functions of the mind and mental factors would not arise.
The Master Mi said: "It is as if within a single mountain there were much copper and iron," extending up to the eighteen realms (*dhātu*). This is intended to provide an analogy;

having already established the similarity with the great realm (*mahādhātu*), he says: "Just as within a single mountain there is much copper, iron, gold, and silver, these must first have the species of copper and so forth for copper and the others to exist.
If the species did not first exist, then copper and the others would not exist. At this point...
It is the same for the eighteen elements within the body. Only by virtue of having a prior homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) do the eighteen elements exist;
if there were no homogeneous cause, then those eighteen elements would not exist. What is called a "homogeneous cause"? Answer: It is like the preceding moment of visual consciousness.
The faculty of the eye immediately preceding draws in the faculty of the eye of the subsequent moment; thus, the preceding faculty of the eye is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for it.

As it is with the eye, so it is with the other faculties as well. Regarding the term "realm" (*dhātu*), its meaning is that of a "lineage" (*gotra*). Question: What is the meaning of "lineage"? Answer: "Lineage" has the meaning of being the "source of birth.
Question: In what sense does it mean "source of birth"? Answer: "Source" refers to the location of the faculty (*indriya-sthāna*). Now, this "realm" [is defined by this].
Because they can produce subsequent moments of the faculties, it is said that the explanation of the *dhātus* (elements) has the meaning of being the basis for production.

[The Master] Mi says: "Regarding these eyes and so forth, up to the point where they are called 'homogeneous causes' (*sabhāga-hetu*), the intention is to demonstrate that the *dhātus* are able to produce the faculties."
"Dhātu" (element) refers to the aforementioned homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*); "indriya" (faculty) refers to the faculty of the subsequent moment.

Therefore, it is said that "dhātu" has the meaning of "arising. That is to say, "dhātu" is that which can produce; because it can produce mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), it is termed "meaning" (*artha*).
Relying on this interpretation, it is clearly understood that there is a distinction between "dhātu" and "indriya."
The Master Bi said: "Regarding 'the other three types of skillfulness,' the intent is as follows: there are ten types of treatise masters who possess skillfulness.

Those who deal with the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth—'so forth' here including the seven categories of dependence (*apekṣā*)—deal only with the faculties (*indriya*), the truths (*satya*), and so on. Within the four sections of the treatise, three are combined in total to constitute seven;
the latter three do not correspond [to those categories], and therefore they are established as the 'others. Question: What are these 'other three types of skillfulness'? Answer: The others..."

The third [category] refers precisely to the vehicles (*yāna*) as well as the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The subsequent verse states, "Based on this, the method is established.
Regarding the term "or four skillful means" (*catur-kuśala*), the intended meaning is that this is explained according to the seven skillful means;

since the *Abhidharmakośa* mentions "aggregates" (*skandha*) and so forth, the "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the four [categories] beginning with the truths for those of middling faculties. Thus, it says "or four. This is based on those skillful means.

Regarding "names": they exist collectively in relation to the household. When it is now said that there are "the remaining three or four," these are all spoken from the perspective of those who have turned their minds [toward enlightenment].
As for the statement by Mi: "One who attains the name of the creator"—this intends to mean that the created [phenomena] can attain the name of the creator.
The Secret [Commentary] says: "The answer is simply that there is no [separate] clothing. Regarding the statement, "As for the function of the grasper and the grasped," the intent is as follows:

Although the aspect (*nimitta*) arises dependent upon consciousness, it is nonetheless the function of the grasper and the grasped within consciousness itself. Furthermore, because it is directly apprehended by consciousness, for these many reasons, the aspect and the seeing (*darśana*) are not identical to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
It cannot be argued that the seeing is the consciousness while the aspect is its function; rather, the aspect is the function because it is what is directly apprehended.

The Secret [Commentary] says: "From 'explaining distinct seeds' up to 'of the same kind,' the intended meaning is as follows: Even if one were to grant that the seeds of the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) exist separately from one another, these too are transformations of consciousness.
Why? Because it is said that the seeing-part and the image-part belong to the same category of support (*āśraya*) as described by the Master [Vasubandhu]."

The Master Mi says: "Furthermore, because it is the direct object of appropriation by the function of consciousness" means that the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) also functions upon the self-verifying-part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*).
"Direct object of appropriation" refers to the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), for it is the direct object of appropriation by the seeing-part.
Among the four parts, one does not allow for the seeing-part to be separated from or to mediate between itself and the object; rather, it directly perceives the image.
The Secret [Commentary] says: "Based on the seventh [consciousness], it is said that its name applies to all three natures. The meaning is this:

because the fundamental ignorance associated with the seventh consciousness serves as the root, the ignorance of the first six consciousnesses is able to increase and act as a condition, giving rise to the mind and mental factors of the three natures.
Furthermore, due to the ignorance of the seventh consciousness, the first six consciousnesses cannot be withdrawn; therefore...
Regarding the statement that the branch of ignorance (*avidyā*) pervades all three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*):

the *Miji* (Secret Commentary) states, "In accordance with the established doctrine of the twelvefold dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), it is said to pervade the three natures. The intended meaning is as follows:

according to the Sarvāstivāda masters, who analyze [phenomena] based on their conformity to suchness (*tathatā*), ignorance is neutral (*avyākṛta*); thus, all five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and all constituent elements (*dhātu*) therein are [encompassed].
It is called the limb of ignorance (*avidyā*). Why? Because it abides in the state of the limb of ignorance. The same applies to the other limbs;
therefore, it is said that the limb of ignorance permeates all three natures.
The Secret [Commentary] states: "The attachment to phenomena (dharma-grāha) extends throughout all three natures" means that the attachment to phenomena serves as the ground for ignorance;

thus, within the minds of the three natures, there is always attachment. Because this attachment within the minds of the three natures acts as a condition, ignorance likewise extends throughout all three natures.
This is the interpretation according to Master Sthiramati. Dharmapāla does not permit [the presence of] wholesome minds [in this context].
There is a point of contention here.

[Master] Mi said: "Regarding the statement that the seventh [consciousness] is without marks (*animitta*) and reaches the stage of the 'limbs of existence' (*bhavāṅga*)," the intended meaning is this:

If the seventh consciousness, being without marks, were to pervade the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and be designated as the limb of ignorance (*avidyā*), how could that seventh ignorance be capable of producing the general and specific karmic retributions? Indeed...
It is only when ignorance gives rise to both general and specific karmic retributions that it can be designated as the "limb of ignorance.
Since the seventh [link], ignorance, cannot give rise to general and specific karma, how could it receive the name "limb of ignorance"? Therefore, one should know that this is incorrect.

The Secret [Commentary] says: "If it is because the five aggregates in the state of ignorance (avidyā) pertain to all three moral natures when associated with the wholesome and so forth, [and thus constitute the link of volitional formations (saṃskāra)]," the meaning is this:

if you say that there is a veneration [of this view], claiming that within the stage of ignorance the five aggregates pervade the three natures—and therefore the link of ignorance pervades the three natures—that is not so.

If one says that the five aggregates in the stage of the link of ignorance pervade the three natures, then being simultaneous with the wholesome and unwholesome natures would mean they are already the link of volitional formations.
Therefore, how can it be called the "ignorance" (*avidyā*) member? Thus, we know that this is incorrect.

As for [Master] Mi’s statement, “The person who participates does not distinguish,” the intended meaning is that other people take the ignorance of the seventh consciousness as the substance of the member.
In the present system of dharma-practice, the seventh ignorance serves as the remote condition for the arising of the ignorance associated with the six consciousnesses.
Only when this [latter] ignorance is able to incite karma is it termed "branch-karma. The seventh ignorance is designated as a "branch" because it functions as a remote condition;
there is no distinction made regarding other persons, yet there is a difference [in their application].
The Secret [Commentary] says: "Now, regarding the fact that the *Mūla* [Abhidharma-kośa-bhāṣya] speaks only of 'I' as the one who explains, the intention is this:

it refers to this capacity to know the faculties (*indriya*) and so forth, and to perceive and cognize objects. Therefore, 'I' is spoken of as the one who can explain; it does not mean that the substance of the 'I' is identical with the act of seeing.
To conceive of volition (*cetanā*) as the 'I' is [the view of] the Saṃmitīyas."
The Master Mi said: "That which is able to calculate and that which is calculated constitute the three divisions. Regarding the phrase "the seeing [division] is the locus of designation":
this means that the seeing division (darśana-bhāga) designates a self and dharmas upon the object-division (nimitta-bhāga);
therefore, it is said that the seeing division is the agent of designation, while the object-division is the locus of designation. It is like designating a path within a palace.
The site is the locus where the house is constructed; the people are those who construct it. When we now speak of "self and dharmas," it is based on these two parts [the grasper and the grasped];
this is the intended meaning. As for your statement that "the pervasive conceptualizer reaches the nature of the grasped," the meaning is this:
because the nature of the grasped self and dharmas is designated upon the basis of the two parts—the pervasive conceptualizer and the object of conceptualization.
The Secret [Commentary] says: "This is because it is the subject that perceives, appearing as if it were the object of attachment. The meaning is this:
If one does not conceive of the self as the perceiving subject (*ālambaka*), then one may simply designate the self and phenomena (*dharma*) based upon the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*).

Even if one grants that the self is conceived as the perceiving subject, why not designate the self and phenomena based upon the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*)? For what reason? Because the subjective aspect is the perceiving subject, appearing as if it were the object.
The intended meaning is that "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) is the subjective perceiver (*ālambaka*), in which the semblance of a real self (*ātman*) as falsely grasped appears.
By this principle, it is also appropriate to designate the self and phenomena (*ātmadharma*) based upon the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) within the present cognitive object.
The Secret [Commentary] says: "If it were based solely on the aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), even to the point where they are entirely dissimilar. This means:

if one were to allow that the grasping for a self is based solely upon the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*), this would be impossible for that which is based on and conditioned by [the subject]. Why? Because the objective aspect and the grasping self that is the subjective perceiver (*ālambaka*)—[are entirely dissimilar]."
This is not analogous. Generally speaking, all that constitutes the objective part (*nimitta-bhāga*) cannot serve as an object of cognition.

For this reason, it is logically clear that the assertion of a self based on the visual consciousness (*darśana-bhāga*) is taken as its object. Although the eighth consciousness is the objective part of the seventh consciousness, it nonetheless cannot be perceived by it.
As for the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) manifested upon consciousness, none of them can serve as an object of cognition.
[The Master] Mi said: "The *Śatadharma-vidya-mukha-śāstra* speaks of only two aspects" means that the *nimitta-bhāga* and the *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect) are what are called the "two aspects.

When it says in the world that "there are no objects," it means that there is only consciousness and the absence of external objects. The term "aspects" (*artha*) mentioned below refers to the same thing.
According to this explanation, [Master] Mi says:
"Because the two parts are distinct" means that the two divisions of the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) are called the "two consciousnesses.

Since the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) does not depart from the conditions, it is also called "consciousness. That the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) is named "consciousness" is a principle that is fully established.

The *Miji* (Secret Commentary) states: "Regarding the appearance of the object-aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) transformed by the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) as if it were the subject-aspect (*grāhaka-lakṣaṇa*)," this means that when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) takes as its object the eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) arising simultaneously with itself, it designates the mental consciousness as the "subject.

At that very moment, when the seeing-part of the mental consciousness conversely takes the eye-consciousness as its subject, the eye-consciousness that is being grasped is also subsumed under the object-aspect. Therefore, [the status of being a subject] depends solely upon the object-aspect.
This is because it grasps at a self and dharmas. The same applies to the seventh consciousness as it takes the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as its object.

Regarding this, the *Mishū* (Secret Commentary) states: "One interpretation says 'resembling' (*sadṛśa*). As explained in the *Shi*, the meaning is that when the self-witnessing (*svasaṃvitti*) transforms, it gives rise to the seeing-part and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) according to the principle of arising;
why then is the word 'resembling' further added? The answer is: When it is said that [the consciousness] "transforms resembling the two parts," it is stated...

The "two parts" (dvaya) grasped by oneself are like the real perceived object (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiving subject (*darśana-bhāga*) as imagined by false conceptualization; therefore, the term "like" (*sadṛśa*) is used.

It is not said that self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) is like the perceived object and the perceiving subject; rather, it is simply stated that the perceived object and the perceiving subject are like the two parts grasped through pervasive conceptual construction (*parikalpita*).

How is it said that they are "similar"? Answer: Although the two parts of the parikalpita (the imagined nature) lack any real substance, they both pertain to false attachment as real grasper and grasped.
Because they are understood through the similarity between grasper and grasped, they are called "similar."
The Secret [Commentary] says: "If one takes the 'grasping subject' as the basis, how does this differ from the 'protection of phenomena'? The intended meaning is this:

when the self-cognizing true transformation serves as the basis for the other-dependent, it manifests as two parts that resemble the self-cognizing part. If one grasps these two parts as being real, only then do they constitute the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

If its essence is non-existent, how does this differ from the Dharma-protector (Dharmapāla)? The Dharma-protector also states that if one clings to the characteristics of the seeing [consciousness] as being substantially real, that too is a parikalpita (imagined nature).
Thus, he speaks of "firmly clinging to the seeing and the characteristics. If [you claim] that the myriad things have no essence, how does this differ from the Dharma-protector?

The Secret Commentary says: "That which is capable of conceptualization is entirely what is grasped by one's own adherence. This means that these subjects and objects of conceptualization are not the conceptualizations of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the thoroughly imagined nature);
rather, they are merely conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and discursive thoughts, which are also considered forms of conceptualization.

The *Biji* says: "To have no basis in existence yet forcibly posit two kinds of semblances of existence" means: "Non-existence" refers to the self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*); "existence" refers to one's own attachment;

"the essence of existence" refers to self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*); and "forcibly positing" refers to the self and phenomena. Although self-realization is not the self or phenomena, one forcibly designates the self and phenomena upon that very essence.
This refers to the conceptualization of the self and phenomena based upon the essence of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
This refers to the simultaneous presence of the protector [Maitreya] and the wise [Sthiramati]. This applies to the "pseudo-self.

As for Sthiramati, regarding the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), he does not apply this name to the two aspects—the self and phenomena—because both the seeing and the seen lack substantial reality.

The Secret [Commentary] states: "Regarding this being identical in meaning though different in name to the second explanation in the *Mūla-ṭīkā*, the intent is that it accords with the second of the two explanations by Sthiramati found within this commentary."
Bimi said: "Virtue" refers to Great Virtue (Mahāśrī), which is none other than Master Zonglun. Bimi said:

As for those who personally received his instructions, it was Master Ji who personally participated in the translation, taking up the pen to compose the text. How could he not have known the school of Sthiramati?
[He would have known that] the self and dharmas are established based upon the two divisions of the parikalpita-svabhāva; how could he not have known that self-cognition takes as its object...?
"There is no teacher. Thus, one knows that the commentary rejects the former interpretation.
Regarding [Dao]mi’s statement, "How could those who have not yet studied speak on the same level? the meaning is as follows: Dharma Master Chongfu was a scholar under Dharma Master Ji;
therefore, he says "those who have not yet studied. As for "on the same level," the meaning is: since they have not yet studied, how could they possibly be on the same level as other dharma masters?
"Are you also contending for fame at the same time?
Bi replied, "It is just like the three commentaries on the Spring and Autumn Annals (*Chunqiu*). Those who race their chariots against Qiuming (Zuoxiang) are the three commentators;
however, this single work was originally spoken by Confucius himself, and it was annotated by the two masters Gong and Lianggu. This was the original intent.
Although it is but one [text], it is called the "Three Transmissions" (Sanzhuan) according to the three persons involved.
As for the "Expositor of the Sūtra" (Yanjingzhe), this refers to the commentaries and transmissions of Gong and Liang. The remaining two, Gong and Liang, were scholars of Confucius;
how could they be ranked as teachers of equal standing with Kong Qiu? How could it be that Confucius was not right while the other two were?
The Secret [Master] said: Regarding the question, "In the school of Sthiramati, do all [cognitions] possess the two parts? the intended meaning is as follows:
In the school of Sthiramati, it is reckoned that the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*) are themselves the object-condition (*ālambana*).

If the cognizing consciousness (*vijñāna*) clings to these grasper and grasped as being substantially real, only then are they the two parts of the seeing and the appearance (*darśana-bhāga* and *nimitta-bhāga*). Their essence is non-existent; it is not the case that all minds take both [parts] as their object.
Furthermore, if one does not take the two types of grasping as objects, how can consciousness possess both parts?
Since one does not conceive of the two types of grasping as real, how could the two parts arise? Such is the meaning of the question.

The Secret [Commentary] says: "The answer regarding the meaning of 'existence' has distinctions. The intent is this: this "meaning of existence" briefly adopts the position of Master Sthiramati to answer the question posed by the previous master.
The answer states: "In general, according to whatever is conceptualized, the object is not necessarily simultaneous with the mind.

For this reason, it is known that when explaining the distinctions of all minds as they take objects, there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*). The first permutation concerns the five [sensory consciousnesses] and the eighth [ālayavijñāna]."
Although consciousness possesses the aspect (*nimitta*), it does not necessarily possess the seeing (*darśana*) portion. The remaining phrases can be understood accordingly.
However, although the sixth consciousness likewise possesses both portions, its aspect and seeing portions do not necessarily arise simultaneously with the mind.
This explains the distinction between various minds as they perceive objects—whether they arise together or not—and this constitutes the general summary of the intended response.
The Secret [Commentary] says: "Regarding 'answering the question without dispatching it,' this means that although one provides an answer, one does not resolve the question.

The Secret [Commentary] says: "Furthermore, 'that which is not directed toward the actual point' means that this does not accord with the original intent of the question. The intended meaning is as follows:

according to Master Sthiramati, for a consciousness that acts as the perceiver (*ālambaka*) to be called "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*), it must necessarily perceive an object (*ālambana*) and grasp both the perceived and the perceiver as real entities. Only then is it termed pervasive.
Regarding the "two parts" as they are conceptually grasped: if consciousness within them does not take the two apprehensions (grāhya-grāhaka) as its object, how could there be two parts?
Such is the intent of the question. Now, regarding the distinction between being about to engage with an object and not yet being so engaged—how would this correspond to what was asked previously?
Therefore, it is said that [the two parts] do not exist at the time of engagement.
Bimi said: "To say that 'it is not excluded' up to this point means: his [the opponent's] original question was regarding the cause for the production of the two parts.

Based on whether they currently abide or not, he replied: 'The cause for the production of the two parts is merely their characteristic. Yet, how can there be a distinction between seeing them together or not together?
Since one is deluded by the same [conclusion] as the opponent previously held, it is said that 'this is not excluded.'"
The *Miji* (Secret Commentary) says: "Now, it is further explained that 'arising in the latter two parts' means this is the interpretation of the *Miji* school.

Regarding 'in either one of them,' it means that when a contaminated consciousness (*sāsrava-vijñāna*) arises as a transformation, both the subjective grasper (*grāhaka*) and the objective grasped (*grāhya*) are present; if either of these two parts were missing, [the consciousness would not arise]."
It is impossible for the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) to arise without the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*). Therefore, whenever a consciousness arises, both parts are produced simultaneously.
It cannot be as Sthiramati maintains—that there first exist the objective referent (*ālambana*) and the seeing and image-parts by nature, and only thereafter do the subsequent two parts arise.

This [view] that the objective referent and the grasped-grasping (the seeing and image-parts) are real entities is a clinging to the object of cognition. Thus, these grasped and grasper aspects—the seeing and image-parts—are substantially existent.
These two parts, which are the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), are what is meant by the "arising of the latter two parts.

As for the secret teaching [of Vasubandhu] stating that he answered Ananta (An-hui) regarding the point that "it cannot be established as a valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*): the intended meaning is that Ananta should simply have separated the root text from the commentary and treated them as two distinct works.
It does not necessarily mean that the statement that the eyes and so forth are direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) constitutes a valid cognition. Therefore...
"Now it does not take [the object] as its condition. Mi said:
"One should say 'expectant grasping' (*ābhoga-grahaṇa*). As for 'reaching the present,' the meaning is this:

although all [cognitions] involve grasping, that which has light grasping is called direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), whereas that which has heavy grasping is called non-direct perception (*aprtyakṣa*). Another interpretation states: According to Sthiramati’s reckoning, regarding the eight contaminated consciousnesses (*sāsrava-vijñāna*):
All of these are attachments to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). If one follows this principle, they would all be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). [The author] says:
"Regarding 'that which is wholesome in the ultimate and conventional sense,' the intended meaning is as follows: if it is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is called wholesome in the ultimate sense;

if it is tainted (*sāsrava*), it is called wholesome in the conventional sense, because it is established through characteristics such as a vase. This too may be considered wholesome in the conventional sense when contrasted with the imaginary nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)."
These are called "wholesome. In contrast to the untainted (*anāsrava*) and ultimate wholesome dharmas, they may also be termed "unwholesome.

Regarding the statement, "This is based on the first meaning; it can be understood through reflection," the intention is as follows: Master Sthiramati says that the two parts—the perceived (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiving (*darśana-bhāga*)—are conceptually imputed (*parikalpita*).
Furthermore, since the self and phenomena do not exist, this refers to the non-existence of things, which is the non-existence of the dependent (*paratantra*).
The Secret [Commentary] says: "Regarding the phrase 'speaking in terms of the preeminent,' the intended meaning is as follows:

if one were to speak exclusively from the perspective that [the object] is not real, then one would merely be speaking of the realm of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*) as being preeminent in its ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), while asserting that the aspect of the object (*nimittabhāga*) is unreal. Therefore, it is known that this is not spoken according to the four types of ultimate truth.
If it were spoken according to the four types of ultimate truth, then one would simply take the name of the jar as the ultimate truth, rather than speaking in terms of its preeminence."
Furthermore, because this is discussed in terms of its preeminent excellence, it differs from what preceded.
Regarding the statement, "Based on being separated from the aggregates, up to being included within the category of the cause of dharmas," the intended meaning is as follows:

Since the imagined self—which is conceived as pervasive and eternal—lacks any substantial essence, it is therefore subsumed under the category of *dharmasādhāraṇa* (the commonality of dharmas). If, however, it refers to the appearances such as blue and so forth that are transformations of consciousness, they appear to exist...

Because it is the substance (*svabhāva*), it is not subsumed within the "homogeneous class" (*sabhāga*) of phenomena; rather, it follows the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*), and is thus subsumed within the four aggregates (*skandha*).
Therefore, the two types are distinct. Although they are of one kind in being "aspects" (*nimitta*), there is a distinction between that which possesses substance and that which lacks it.

Furthermore, another explanation states: although the aspects transformed by the six consciousnesses are non-existent, there are many distinctions among the substances of jars; however, only one kind is subsumed within the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*).
Apart from consciousness, there is no intrinsic nature; that which is the object of the mind is of one kind, being equally subsumed under the category of *dharmas* and *sabhāga*.
Although there are two interpretations, according to the principles of reasoning, the former interpretation is superior.
The Secret Record states: "Fuxi had a serpent’s body and an ox’s head. 'Serpent’s body' means that this person’s body possessed serpent scales;
'ox’s head' means that his body possessed an ox’s head. He was the Son of Heaven in ancient times. However, regarding Fuxi as described in the books:"
There are three [names]. First is Fuxi; second is Mimi; third is Baofxi. Why is he named Fuxi?
"Fu" (伏) carries the meaning of subduing. Because he was able to subdue all wild beasts, he is called Fu.
What is meant by “Xi”? “Xi” refers to the sacrificial offerings (*śikṣā*). One who is able to subdue [them] is named Fuxi. Fuxi is thus Jiaomi Xi.
“Mi” (subtle/dense) means that this Fuxi is able to practice what is subtle and dense; because he practices it, he is called Mi Xi. Mi Xi is the *Jiemimi* (Kṣemamkara).

As for insects, birds, and so forth, those named Fuxi are— (Note: The provided source text contains numerous lacunae and illegible characters. The translation above reconstructs the likely intended meaning based on standard Buddhist and Chinese cosmological terminology, specifically regarding the figure Fuxi and his association with the subtle and the sacrificial rites.)
"Jun" (君) is a title. Why is he named Pao-xi (庖羲)? "Pao" (庖) means kitchen.

Because he was able to cause cooked food—such as rice and other prepared meals—to be easily produced within the kitchen, he received the name Pao-xi based on this meaning. Question: As for the word "Xi" (羲), there are three types:
first, sunlight is called Xi; second, the personal name Xi is called Xi; third, Xi refers to the character "Han" (罕). Since there are these three [uses]..."
Question: Why is the first or second "Xi" (羲) not used, but rather the third "Xi" character?
Answer: The other two "Xi" characters each pertain to specific matters; only the third "Xi" character encompasses and applies to many types [of beings].
Question: How did people exist before Fuxi appeared? Answer: They each dwelt in their respective caves; they lived in their solitary burrows and had no houses.
Regarding dwellings: it was only after Fuxi appeared that houses were first constructed. Before Fuxi’s appearance, there were no written characters or seals;
they relied solely on knotted cords for communication. Once Fuxi was born, there ought to have been written characters and seals.
Prior to Fuxi’s arrival, all the various beasts could not be subdued by humans. It was because Fuxi was born that he was able to bring all [beasts] under control.
A beast that is able to subdue oxen and ride horses, drawing heavy loads to distant places; because of these many capabilities, it obtains the name "Fú-xī" (伏羲).

This is precisely why the character for "xiù" (秀, excellence) is placed below the character for "yì" (義, righteousness). Question: For what reason is this specific meaning alone used to place the character "xiù" beneath "yì"?
Answer: "Yì" is also called "shí" (real/substance). To discard the flowery and adhere to the substantial is what is meant by "xiù. Now, as for this meaning of "subduing" (伏), its essence is...
Flowers preserve their movement toward the attainment of fruit; this is why they are subdued by the name "Yi" (Righteousness).

One uses only this character "Yi," and not the other two characters "Xi. Question: As for the term "Fu Yi" (Subduing Righteousness), is it a name or is it his nature? Answer: It is neither a name nor a surname.
Because he was able to subdue beasts and other creatures, he received the name Fuxi. Fu Yi’s original surname was Feng, and his given name was Ren.
Therefore, he was titled "Wind-Poet" (Fengren). In former times, names were distinguished by one's clan name; nowadays, people establish names separately from their clan names.

For example, when poets take the character *xi* (sacrificial ox) from the word *niuxi* (ox-colored sacrificial ox), they do so solely based on the meaning of the animal "ox" (*niu*) within the clan name *Fu* (Fuxi). Thus, he is named Fuxi.
The Secret Master said: "Regarding the argument that the treatise points to 'eternal emptiness' (常空) as a metaphor, the intention is this:
according to the masters of the treatise, there are two kinds of emptiness—first, eternal emptiness; second, impermanent emptiness (無常空).
Now, since the treatise points to eternal emptiness as the metaphor, there is no fault of the probandum being unestablished within the example."
The Secret Master said: "Regarding the statement 'first establish emptiness as permanent,' your intention is that if you claim emptiness is impermanent, there is a fault within your analogy.
Now, having first established emptiness as permanent, how can you then cite me extensively as a similar example?"
Bodhidharma said: "Regarding 'universally and eternally pervasive,' if one speaks of it in a general sense, the term 'universally and eternally pervasive' is indeed accepted.
However, if one clings to a self as being eternally and universally pervasive, the Mahāyāna does not accept this."
The Secret Commentary says: "Regarding the statement 'there are those who employ the term "adherence" (執),' the intent is as follows:

those capable of adhering to the terminology [of logic]—namely, those who understand *hetuvidyā* (logic)—universally agree that the term 'adherence' applies to both the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)."

The Secret [Commentary] says: "To say it is entirely a fabrication" means that the *Śāstra* contains the word "adherence" (*xié*) while the *Vyākhyā* contains the word "allowance" (*xǔ*); the two meanings are identical.
This is why the *Śāstra* uses only the word "adherence" and does not include the word "allowance. Why then is there a need to explain *Hetuvidyā*?

Regarding the statement, "Is it in accordance with what is commonly accepted regarding the cause and the example, or is it in accordance with the words of those who hold [specific] views?"—if one interprets it in this way, it is merely a hollow claim that renders it devoid of logical principle.
Beiji says: "The dimensions of the large and the small are equal" means that, for instance, a single visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) consists of seven atoms (*paramāṇu*). These...
Regarding atoms (*paramāṇu*): even when they are compared with one another, their dimensions are equal; yet they are not the "producers" (*bhūta*) and the "produced" (*bhautika*).

The produced elements are also compared with one another and are said to be "equal in dimension. However, it is only when the seven producers and the seven produced are each naturally compared with one another that they are called "equal.
Question: Why do the producers and the produced not transform into one another, such that they are both mutually related and compared with one another? Answer:
It is not so; they differ in size. That which is the creator is called the *paramāṇu* (extreme atom), while that which is created is called the *aṇu* (atom).

Since there is a difference in size, they cannot be called "equal" and so forth. Therefore, this is stated solely by comparing the creators with one another and the created with one another. The intended meaning is:
when it is said that the seven *paramāṇus* of the creator, such as the earth element, are equal to the created, this establishes each individual *paramāṇu* by comparing them with one another.

The *Mishuo* (Secret Explanation) says: "That which can create the earth-element (*pṛthivī-mahābhūta*)" means that the six things, such as the eye, are called the "created" (*bhautika*), while only the single earth-element is called the "creator" (*bhūta*).

Question: Since all great sense organs, such as the eye, employ the four pure great elements (*catvāri śuddha-mahābhūtāni*), why is it that regarding the "created," only the earth-element is mentioned and not the other three great elements?
Answer: According to the underlying principle, one should also mention the other three great elements here.

However, because the earth element constitutes the eye faculty and so forth, and its characteristics are most prominent, it is mentioned specifically. Furthermore, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it says:
"Just as with the five faculties, there are those composed of one great element, two great elements, and even three or four great elements;
yet upon obtaining the future state, they necessarily become a single faculty, all fully possessing the four great elements."
The Secret [Commentary] states: "Seven atoms in one place" means that the seven substances, such as the eye and so forth, each possess their own distinct atoms, yet they abide in the same location;
therefore, it is said that "seven atoms are in one place."

The Secret [Commentary] says: "The pervasive capacity can produce six. This means that within a single element of earth (pṛthivī-mahābhūta), there are six functional capacities for producing derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) and so forth;
thus, while the producer is one, the produced has six aspects.
The Secret [Master] said: "It is not so created. Why are there six distinctions? This means:
if one says that the creator is only one, how can that which is created be six?
The Secret [Commentary] says: "Those of the same category as earth" means that for the seven substances, such as the eye, there are likewise seven corresponding primary elements (bhūta).
Since they share the same category as earth, only one instance of the earth element is mentioned; however, in reality, there are seven earth elements.
The Master Mi said: "Regarding the statement that 'a single eye is composed of seven atoms,' when it is said according to the classification of types, the meaning is as follows:
although the eye is constructed from immeasurable and numerous atoms, the mention of the seven substances—form, odor, and so forth—is spoken according to their types.

As for the principle that this eye-faculty is all constructed from seven atoms, it is likewise the case that there are actually seven instances of the earth-element (pṛthivī-mahābhūta), because the earth-element is..."
Because they are identical, only one "earth" (dhātu) is mentioned.

Regarding the statement, "In a single subtle point of a sense-faculty, seven substances co-reside," the intended meaning is as follows: for instance, a single eye-faculty is composed of seven substances.

Within those seven substances, even within the minute dimension of the eye-faculty itself, there are likewise seven subtle points that co-reside; namely, the eye-faculty itself [and its six associated elements].

The "house" (*gṛha*) can form subtle particles (*paramāṇu*). Together with the other six subtle particles such as fragrance, they constitute seven. Thus, it is clearly understood that each of the seven substances, such as visible form (*rūpa*), consists of seven subtle particles.
Seven times seven makes forty-nine subtle particles; therefore, the text below states: "By means of these seven subtle particles, one corresponds to those seven subtle particles.
Just as the eye already possesses seven subtle particles, so too do fragrance and the others collectively possess seven subtle particles each. As for the remainder...
It may be inferred from this. Therefore, it is said that these seven [atoms] and those seven [atoms] dwelling in the same location are called "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*).

As for the statement that "the seven-sevens are each distinct," the intended meaning is as follows: the forty-nine atoms previously mentioned—seven times seven—are each individually separated, yet they coexist in their very substance;
this is called "intermingling" (*miśra*).
The Secret [Commentary] says: The third fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states, "That which is blended and not separated.

The intent is that this citation serves as proof for the preceding meaning. Question: The second [section] clarifying names speaks of "separation and non-separation. Why does the citation used as proof instead speak of "blending and separation"?
Answer: It is merely a difference in terminology; the meaning is of one kind.

The Secret Commentary (*Bimi*) states: "That these great elements (*mahābhūta*), as atoms (*paramāṇu*), and other aggregations reach the same location" means that, for example, the earth element, in relation to other things such as fragrance, shares the same location as visible form (*rūpa*).
Thus, other substances such as fragrance and taste are called "other aggregations.
When these substances, such as fragrance and so forth, are considered in relation to one another, they are all capable of being termed "aggregations."
This refers precisely to the primary elements and their derivatives. Because it is observed as something distinct from other colors and so forth, it is called a "collection of the rest.
Furthermore, if there is a collection, it is designated by names such as "sesame" or "beans," and yet there is still a collection present.

The term "held by the secret" (*hiji*) means that the three factors—such as glue and so forth—each individually have the capacity to hold substances such as hemp, just as medicinal pills are held together by being bound with a secret agent.
Furthermore, it refers to hemp and beans being in one place, or hemp fibers being in one place.
One cannot mix hemp and beans into a single entity.
[The opponent] says: "That which is distinct from the great elements (mahābhūta) [is the derived matter]. Hemp and beans each have their own distinct great elements.
[The opponent] says: "Regarding the combination of the three aggregates, one should say that honey, glue, and sand—these three aggregates—are each capable of maintaining [their own form]."
"Many beans and so forth constitute a single location.
[Master] Mi said: "Because distinct accumulations face one another, they are called 'conjunction' (saṃnipāta).
This means that although they are all equally beans, because the number of individual grains is great, they are termed "distinct accumulations"; that is, each grain faces those other grains.
The Secret [Commentary] says: "As for 'if one takes the aggregates themselves to be the self,' the intention is as follows:

For instance, when non-Buddhists speak of taking the aggregates themselves to be the self, this is merely the Buddha’s Dharma describing how others conceive of a self, stating that it is 'identical with the aggregates. This is said in contrast to the fundamental conception of those non-Buddhists, who do not establish the aggregates [as a distinct category].
Now, when it is said that 'the self is identical with the aggregates,' this is the formal presentation of the Buddha’s Dharma; therefore, it is a conception of the self."
As for this "volition" (*cetanā*), it should be said that it is included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).

Regarding the statement "it should be so," the secret meaning is as follows: although they are of one kind and identical in being matter (*rūpa*), when viewed from the perspective of their categories, they are distinguished as manifest action (*vijñapti*) and non-manifest action (*avijñapti*).
Since these are distinct categories, they must be refuted separately.

Regarding the statement, "It cannot be said that it is not-self," which fails to shift when compared to the analogy of a tortoise’s hair: the intended meaning is that tortoise’s hair is indeed not-self;
since you now state that it cannot be said to be "not-self," it is clear that the argument does not apply to the analogy. Tortoise...

Hairs can indeed be described as "not-self. Now, since the word "ineffable" itself cannot be described as "not-self," it is clear that [the reason] does not apply to the example of what is describable.
If the word "ineffable" did not exist, then [the reason] would indeed apply. Thus, the hare’s hair is used as an example of what is describable.
Because [the self] is non-self, [the opponent] says:
"The self must certainly be the aggregates. This means that these are all words of objection. He asserts that while the self is not the essence of the aggregates, it is only real;
thus, although he says the aggregates are not the self, they must certainly be the aggregates and should not be considered non-aggregates. This is stated in view of the tenets of other schools.

My "self" is not the same as those who conceive of a self as being entirely distinct from the aggregates; therefore, this ineffable self must certainly be the aggregates themselves, and it should not be something other than the aggregates.

The Secret [Commentary] says: "This refutation should apply to that which is the aggregates (*skandha*). The intended meaning is: "In this way, one merely refutes the self (*ātman*), but does not refute that which is non-self.
The response says: "It must necessarily be the aggregates, because the self is necessarily the aggregates. Therefore, one merely refutes the self;
as for that which is non-self, it is not the aggregates, and therefore it is not refuted."

The Secret [Commentary] says: "As for 'that which resembles my self,'" the intended meaning is this: it is as if one regards "my self" as the correct conceptualization (*samyak-parikalpa*), while not regarding that which resembles "not-my-self" as such.
Therefore, because "not-my-self" is not the correct conceptualization, it is not refuted.
The Secret [Commentary] says: "Difficult to make the case that the self is identical to the aggregates is analogous to the previous intent. This means:

taking the position that "the self is not identical to the aggregates" as the analogy for the three cases—such as saying "the self is not the self, it is the self"—this is the primary refutation of the claim that "it is not the self. If one says "the aggregates are not the aggregates," then they should be identical to the aggregates;
if they were identical to the aggregates, one would be conceiving of a self within the aggregates. Conversely, if the self were separate from the aggregates, one should not conceive of a self at all.
The Secret Commentary says: "Regarding the statement 'there are two establishments,' what constitutes a correct example?

The meaning is this: the 'two establishments' refer to the probans (*sādhana*) and the probandum (*sādhya*). The thesis (*pakṣa*) is the probandum, and the example-reason (*dṛṣṭāntahetu*) is the probans.
Only when both establishments are present can something qualify as a correct example. If either one of the two establishments is lacking, it cannot be established."
The Master said: "If you were to take the treatise literally, since the treatise does not state that [the self] does not exist within the collection and so forth, the implication is this:
if you were to accept the words of the treatise as definitive, then for instance, the treatise does not say that 'self' exists upon a collection of 'non-self'."

How is it that the present thesis is established? Why is it said that [the person] cannot even be described as being within the collection of aggregates (*skandha*)? Although this is not explicitly stated in the text, the phrasing suggests an implicit meaning.

The intent is, conversely, to clarify that it cannot be described as being "hidden" within the collection of aggregates. Therefore, one should know that it cannot be described as either conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Although the treatise speaks of it in a single location, we shall now distinguish between what is indescribable and what is conditioned or unconditioned.
To explain each separately is not problematic.

As for the phrase "furthermore, for whom" (*yasya punar api*), the intended meaning is: if one does not accept the others, it must be explained whether [the object] is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Since the meaning has already been expressed by the word "furthermore" (*api ca*), why is the phrase "furthermore" (*yasya punar api*) used again? The answer is as follows.
Mipó said: "If one could realize nirvana through the view of self," which means that one can only grasp at nirvana by realizing that the view of self does not take a self as its object.

The Secret [Commentary] says: "If it were the object of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), then it would be subject to negation. The intended meaning is that, according to the non-Buddhist schools (*bāhyaka*), the view of self does not take the self as its object.
As stated in the treatise: "If it were the object of the view of self," therefore we know that it is subject to negation.
The Secret [Commentary] says: "Does this not commit the fault of *sādhya-sama* (proving what is already established)? This means:

if other schools hold that the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) does not arise by taking the self as its object, as is refuted in the treatise, then since all views of self do not take a real entity as their object, does this not commit the fault of *sādhya-sama*? Question:

Generally speaking, the term "view of self" is applied because it arises by taking the self as its object and thus receives the name "view of self. Since it does not arise by taking the self as its object, how can it be called a "view of self"?
"Is it seen? He replied: "There are two kinds of self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). First, the pure self-view, which takes [the self] as an object but does not cling to it.

Second, the defiled self-view, which exclusively takes the self as its object and clings to it firmly. What is now said regarding 'not taking the self as an object' is stated according to the pure self-view;
alternatively, it may be based on the fact that even those non-Buddhists do not admit that self-view takes the self as its object—for instance, the Sāṃkhya school does not."
Granted. The Vaiśeṣika author [claims] that the view of self (ātma-dṛṣṭi) takes a real self as its object; yet even the Vaiśeṣikas do not admit this.
The Sāṃkhya maintains that the view of self arises taking a real self as its object; such various positions, when compared with one another, are all unaccepted.

This statement that "the view of self does not take a real self as its object" is made on this basis. If one considers it from the perspective of our own school, there is no such thing as a view of self.

It does not arise by taking a real self as its object. Although the view of a pure self (*śuddhātma-dṛṣṭi*) and even the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) are not admitted to take a real self as their object, the defiled view of a self (*kliṣṭa-ātmadṛṣṭi*) invariably takes the self as its object.
Since the treatise refutes [the self] based on this defiled view, there is no fault of mutual contradiction.

The Master Mi said: "Regarding the statement 'based on the view of non-defilement,' the intended meaning is as follows: when it was previously stated that the view of selflessness can realize nirvana, this was spoken based on the view of non-defilement regarding the self;
