therefore, it is called the 'view free from defilement. It does not mean that the Path itself is a view free from defilement, nor that there is no defiled practice of the view of self.
Because there exists a defiled view of self, [the question is asked]: 'Furthermore, for instance, as for the view of non-defilement, is this not purity?'"
Question: Since the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is already purified, how can it be said further that one must "leave" it? Can it realize *nirvāṇa*? Answer:
Although the view of self may be purified, if one does not abandon attachment to it, one still generally takes the self as an object and thereby acquires the view of self.

For this reason, it is necessary to challenge the notion that a purified view of self can realize *nirvāṇa*. This is because, as long as there is a defiled view of self, [one cannot attain liberation]. Therefore, it is not...
This refers to the adherence to [the view of] conformity.
Bi said: "The various schools' conceptualizations of a self are all objects of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*). As for the provision of this negation here, the intention is as follows:

This second interpretation states that whatever is conceptualized by the various schools as being 'self' is entirely an object of the view of self; since there is no distinction between defiled and pure [objects], it is known [to be so]."
The treatise states: "If it were not an object of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), this would be a negation. [Master] Mi says:

"It is not called the 'view of self'"; the meaning is that if one understands from what precedes that there are two types of the view of self—namely, the defiled and the pure—and since the pure view of self is also termed the 'view of self,' it is clearly known that the essence of the self is likewise pure.

Regarding the "object-condition of the view" (*dṛṣṭi-ālambana*): how is it that the self-substance (*ātma-bhāva*) of the aforementioned non-Buddhist outsiders is not the object-condition of the view of self? Is this stated with reference to the pure view of self?
Since it is said that the self-substance is not the object-condition of the view of self, it is clearly understood that when the view of self is obstructed, there is an impure understanding of self.
Nor can it be called the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
[Zhi]bi said: "That which penetrates both the ordinary and the sage" means that anything which accords with principle and corresponds to reality is termed the Ultimate Teaching (*zhìjiào*).
"Ultimate" (*zhì*) means reality; it refers to the principle of ultimate reality. Thus, even the Confucianism of the world is included.

The Secret [Commentary] says: "As for the 'Eightfold Category of Speech' (*aṣṭavāg-varga*), it refers to the four so-called 'seeing when one has seen,' 'hearing when one has heard,' 'perceiving when one has perceived,' and 'knowing when one has known';
and the other four, namely 'not seeing when one has not seen,' 'not hearing when one has not heard,' 'not perceiving when one has not perceived,' and 'not knowing when one has not known.

By awakening to the former, the eightfold category of speech is established. Regarding the phrase "the four noble statements" (*catur-ārya-vākya*) and so forth, the intended meaning is as follows: [...]* *Note: The provided source text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the portion available.*
From among the categories of speech (*vāda*), the first four are taken; these constitute the authoritative teaching (*āptāgama*).

Regarding the statement "all are those who practice in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānudharmapratipanna*): the intended meaning is that they are called "practitioners in accordance with the Dharma" because they have heard the Dharma and practice accordingly.
This Dharma is wholesome and capable of being practiced.
The Secret [Commentary] says: Regarding the statement, "If one says that it does not take the self as its object," the meaning is as follows:

There is an interpretation by the Venerable Hakushika (Hokugawa Daide) which states, "If one says that the view of self does not take the self as its object, there is the fault of contradicting what is already established (sādhya-sama). Why is this?
Because even the non-Buddhist schools do not admit that the view of self takes the self as its object; therefore, it commits the fault of being redundant with what is already accepted.

The Secret [Commentary] says: "Regarding those who contradict the Treatise and the Commentary," the meaning is this: both the Treatise and the Commentary state that defiled views take that path as their object and allow for the apprehension of a self.
If one now claims they do not take it as an object, does this not contradict the Treatise and the Commentary?

The Secret [Commentary] says: "If that is so, as for our own school’s position regarding consciousnesses such as that of sound," etc. This means it is stating an external objection. The objection states:

"If the Mahāyāna does not accept my school’s position—that the view of self takes the self as its object—then this would be the Mahāyāna definition of the relationship between the grasper and the grasped."

Neither [position] can be established. The first objection concerns the impossibility of the cognition (*ālambaka*) having an object; the latter objection concerns the impossibility of the object (*ālambana*) itself.
As he himself further stated: "The secret teaching says: Question: To what extent does wisdom not correspond to its object? The intended meaning is this:

If it is said that the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) taking the self as its object is not commonly accepted by the world, and thus one does not admit that it takes the self as its object, then correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) taking suchness (*tathatā*) as its object is likewise not [commonly accepted] by the world. [If you do not admit this,] you must fully admit [the former].
It is understood that, by the same logic, [the fundamental wisdom] should likewise not take *tathatā* (suchness) as its object. How, then, can this objection be refuted? To refute it:

the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is a functional entity (*dharmin*) that certainly does not take *tathatā* as its object. This is the thesis (*pakṣa*). The reason (*hetu*) is: "because it possesses an object. The example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is:

"like the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). If one must elaborate upon the secret objection, it should be formulated according to the preceding method; this refers precisely to the present passage. Question: If the other [party] were to take that seventh... [text fragment].

8. Regarding the objection: What is it? The intention is that this is also an external objection. The objection states: "I see that [the seventh consciousness] takes the self as its object; this is not something universally known in the world.

If you do not grant this, consider for instance how the seventh [consciousness] takes the eighth [consciousness] as its object—how could everyone in the world universally grant that it takes it as an object?

Therefore, the objection continues: "The seventh consciousness certainly does not take the eighth consciousness as its object, because it possesses an object of cognition (*ālambana*), just like the eye and other [senses]."
[The interlocutor] asks: Why do you not raise objections using the other consciousnesses, but instead specifically use the seventh and eighth to raise an objection? [The respondent] answers:
The first six consciousnesses are commonly accepted by the world, whereas only the seventh and eighth are not commonly accepted; therefore, they are cited as the basis for the objection.
The Master Bi said: "Regarding 'among those two treatises,' this refers to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*.

As for the statement that 'there are sixteen kinds of non-Buddhist treatises,' the intention is that within these sixteen kinds of non-Buddhist treatises, the self (*ātman*) is explained, and it is not a portion of the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*)."

The Secret Commentary says: "Therefore, there is no error in the commentary" means that the present [text] merely sets aside the two types of self-view—conceptual and innate—and does not intend to demonstrate its own correct tenets.

The Master Mi said: "Regarding the term 'mixed' (*miśra*), the intended meaning is that although the seventh [consciousness] and its objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) are of one essence, they are called 'mixed' because they are viewed in relation to two distinct characters.

Furthermore, it should be understood that they are termed 'mixed by nature' (*svabhāva-miśra*) because they encompass both the obscured-unwholesome (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) natures."
The Master Mi said: "How could the objective substance (*viṣaya-rūpa*) perceived by the five consciousnesses of that stage be of the same seed? This means:

if one claims that the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective part) of the eye-consciousness in the First Dhyāna is similar to fire in the Desire Realm and therefore draws from the same seed, how can it be that the five consciousnesses of the Desire Realm intersect with [the First Dhyāna] and share the same seed?
Furthermore, for example, when the five objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) intersect, these are the five consciousnesses transformed by the Eighth Consciousness; they do not depend on others.
The eighth point of inquiry: If the primary object itself transforms into its own image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*), how can that image-part be said to "correspond" (*saṃjñā*) to the primary object?

The Secret [Master] says: "To say it 'corresponds' raises doubt. This means: if it does not correspond when belonging to a different stage (*bhūmi*), would it then correspond when belonging to the same stage?
Therefore, he says: "It raises the doubt as to whether it corresponds within the same stage."
The Master Bi said: "Excluding the sixth consciousness, the remaining seven consciousnesses undergo transformation.

This means that each of these seven consciousnesses possesses its own self-verifying portion (svasaṃvitti-bhāga), which transforms and gives rise to the two portions of appearance (nimitta-bhāga) and seeing (darśana-bhāga). These two portions are termed the five aggregates of clinging (pañcopādānaskandha).

However, the sixth consciousness and the co-emergent view of self (sahaja-ātma-dṛṣṭi) take [the objects of] the other seven as their substantial basis (bhūta-vastu); subsequently, they transform and give rise to their own self-characterized portions (sva-nimitta-bhāga) as the reflected image portion (pratibimba-nimitta-bhāga)."
Yet others falsely construct their own interpretations. Question: It may be so for the aggregate of consciousness and the aggregate of form; how is it with the remaining three aggregates? Answer:

Since the remaining three aggregates are mental factors (*caitta*), they likewise each possess a self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) that transforms to give rise to the two divisions of the seeing and the seen (*darśana-nimitta-bhāga*).

As the treatise states: "That which takes as its object the characteristics of the five appropriated aggregates (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) transformed by consciousness" refers precisely to the five appropriated aggregates transformed by the sixth consciousness.

It takes this as its essence. However, this view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) takes these aggregates (*skandha*) as its essence; it arises from the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of its own [consciousness].

Furthermore, according to the Ximing Commentary (*Ximing shu*), it is explained that the five appropriated aggregates (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) comprehensively encompass the eight consciousnesses. Question: What about the seeds of the objective aspects of the five sense-objects (*viṣaya*)?

The five consciousnesses can reach toward a single [object], just as the seeds of the objective essence (*bhāva-bīja*) do. Can consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*) reach toward a single [object]? Answer:

At the sixth stage, the two divisions of appearance and seeing (*nimitta-dṛṣṭi-bhāga*) are now regarded as the objective essence and the summit. Question: For what reason is it called "transformable" (*pariṇāmya*)?

Answer: The seeing and image aspects (*darśana-bhāga* and *nimitta-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses are all produced by the transformation of the self-grasping portion (*sva-abhiniveśa-bhāga*) of those same eight consciousnesses.

The three aggregates (*skandha*) of sensation, perception, and formations (*vedanā*, *saṃjñā*, and *saṃskāra*), which are transformations of that self-grasping, are also described in accordance with the consciousnesses, because they are all designated as having a self-grasping portion.

The Secret [Commentary] asks: "If this is the substantial entity (bhāva), why speak only of that which is transformed by the object-conditioned consciousness? The intention of this question is as follows:

Since the innate view of self (*sahaja-ātma-dṛṣṭi*) within the sixth consciousness arises by taking the five appropriated aggregates (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) as its substantial entity, how can it now be said to take what is transformed by consciousness as its object?

This refers to a remote condition (*viprakṛṣṭa-pratyaya*). The answer is: "In principle, it is also the consciousness that transforms. The intention of this statement is as follows: Although it is said...
Regarding the self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*): its objective essence (*ālambana-svabhāva*) is the aggregates (*skandha*), which is logically identical to that of the other transforming consciousnesses.

How is this so? The answer is: it is necessary for the other seven consciousnesses to first transform and give rise to the five appropriated aggregates (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*); only then can that self-grasping and the like take those aggregates as their objective essence and function as the "self.
This is just as the eighth consciousness transforms and gives rise to the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). As for the five sense objects...

The essential nature (*svabhāva*) serves as the remote objective condition (*parokṣālambanapratyaya*) for the five consciousnesses, while the image (*nimitta*) manifested by itself serves as the immediate objective condition (*pratyakṣālambanapratyaya*). Such is the case.
Regarding the secret point:

the statement that the term "manifested" (*pariṇata*) is used based on both the aspect (*nimitta*) and the seeing (*darśana*) means that although the grasping of a self takes [the object] as its condition, it does not take the essential nature as its object.

Regarding the phrase "the object-condition": it refers to the aspect (nimitta-bhāga) manifested by consciousness. When we speak of that which is manifested, it is said in relation to the distinction between the objective aspect (nimitta-bhāga) and the subjective aspect (darśana-bhāga).

Its substantial basis (vastu) is not the object-condition; rather, it is the aspect manifested by consciousness. Whenever there is a subjective aspect, there must necessarily be an objective aspect. Since it is stated that [consciousness] takes the five appropriated aggregates as its object-condition, there must necessarily be a subjective aspect.

It is not the case that consciousness arises only when it relies upon an external object; therefore, there is an objective aspect. Based on this principle, the term "manifestation" (pariṇāma) was used previously.
Regarding the self-grasping of the provisional and the ultimate: one calculates the essence of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) to be the self.

In principle, that which is directly perceived is only the "aspect" (*nimitta*) that is established. This means that what was stated above regarding the perception of the "essence" (*svabhāva*) is spoken in terms of indirect perception; if one speaks in terms of direct perception, it is only the "objective aspect" (*bhāgākāra*) that is transformed [by consciousness].

The Secret Master said: "If one speaks according to the substantial nature (*dravya*), it is also the transformation of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) that serves as the object-condition. This means that within the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), the four aggregates are, by their very essence, the objects of the fetters.

When it is now said that consciousness grasps the substantial nature of the aggregates as its object-condition, this refers to the transformation of the fetters—the consciousness and so forth—that serve as the object-condition.

It is just as the seventh [consciousness] takes the eighth as its object: the eighth's substantial nature is itself the transformation of the fetters; therefore, the seventh also takes the transformation of the fetters as its object.
"It is a transformation.

Mi said: "This refers to the 'transformed' as explained according to its characteristics. The meaning is that while in reality one speaks of the 'transformed' based on the objective substance (ālambana-pratyaya), it is spoken of here based on the manifestation of its characteristics."

The Secret [Master] said: "In truth, one should also not say that it is transformed by consciousness. The meaning is this: although the term "transformed" is used according to the manifest appearance (*nimitta*), in reality, it only takes the fundamental object (*bhāva*) as its condition;

it does not take what is transformed by consciousness as its condition. Question: Since the five appropriated aggregates (*pañcopādānaskandha*) are already transformed by the other seven consciousnesses, and since the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) subsequently takes them as its object, why do you say it does not take what is transformed by phenomena (*dharma*) as its condition? Answer:
The objective essence (*bhāva*) of the five appropriated aggregates (*pañcopādānaskandha*), etc., which are transformed by the other seven consciousnesses, is precisely what is taken as an object.

However, the image-aspect (*pratibimba-bhāga*) of the aggregates, etc., which are transformed upon those other seven consciousnesses, is not taken as an object. As stated above, all instances where it is said that "that which is transformed by consciousness is not taken as an object" should be understood according to this principle.
The Secret [Commentary] says: "It is not so; if one were to maintain that the object of attachment is what is transformed, one should have used the term 'transformation. The intention is this:

if my position were that the seventh consciousness takes as its object a transformed image, why would it not use the term 'transformation' when the seventh consciousness takes the eighth consciousness as its object? Instead, it merely says, 'taking the eighth consciousness as its object, it gives rise to an image within its own mind.
Therefore, we know that this is spoken with reference to the primary substance (the *bimba*), and does not mean that it takes a transformed image of the consciousness as its object."
Bimi said: "Regarding the previous statement that 'sudden enlightenment is also the Way of Heaven,' the intention was this:

it merely refers to the establishment of the name 'sudden' for those who have attained the first two fruits [of the path], not implying that by having the name 'sudden enlightenment,' one is immediately declared to be a Bodhisattva."

The Master Bi said: "How can one speak of a practitioner who realizes the path of seeing by skipping over the fruits? He asked: "Furthermore, do the masters of the various schools admit the existence of such a person who skips over the fruits?
He replied: "According to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), it is admitted; however, the Mahāyāna does not admit it. Therefore, this will be reconciled below. As the Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya states:

Regarding the explanation of "arising with a fruit," this is based on the teachings of the Hīnayāna. There is a question as to why some do not allow for [the existence of] greed and so forth that are independent (*duh-tuṅ*), as they would lack companions.
Nevertheless, it is admitted that there is such a thing as greed and so forth that are independent yet possess harmful companions. Now, the intent of the commentary is difficult to grasp;
it consistently raises objections concerning companions that *should* accompany greed, rather than raising objections concerning companions of independent greed.
The Secret [Commentary] says: "Regarding the afflictions of the desire realm, since they arise [simultaneously], how can one speak of them as 'prior'? The intention is this:

although the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and its associated greed and so forth cannot be subdued by the sixfold cultivation of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), one does subdue the independent greed and so forth.

Therefore, at the time of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), one also abandons the nine grades of afflictions, including the view of self and others in the desire realm, thereby attaining the third fruit (*phala*). Question: Greed...
Since these [afflictions] are not associated with the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), how can they be called its "companions"? Answer:

Although craving that arises independently does not arise simultaneously with the view of self, because it arises in immediate succession and provides indirect assistance, it is also designated as a "companion.

It is by means of this suppression through the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) that the view of self is severed upon reaching the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Question: The view of self is subtle, yet the afflictions...

Since the mental afflictions (*kleśa*) serve as the basis for their activity and are so powerful, they cannot be severed in a short period of time. How, then, could one suddenly attain the third fruit while still in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*)?
Answer: There are sentient beings in the world who possess either sharp or dull faculties; their lineages and dispositions differ, and there are ten thousand varieties among them.
Some are able to achieve great fruits within a single interval. Why should one harbor doubts about the *anāgāmin*, the lesser sage? It is said that...
Since these sharp-facultied [practitioners] have already subdued [the afflictions] within the six paths of cultivation— namely, the independent greed and so forth,
as well as the remaining eight grades of co-emergent afflictions and the view of self-existence that does not arise now— their modes of activity (*ākāra*) are subtle; therefore,
they are said to abandon them simultaneously with the Path of Seeing and to realize the third fruit.
The Master said: "Furthermore, 'companions' (bàn) refers to those who assist one another. The underlying meaning is this:

if one has the companions of the 'self-view' (ātma-dṛṣṭi) belonging to the schools that hold to [inherent] existence, such as greed and so forth, which are associated with it, then since the fruit and the path are already subtle, how could they possibly subdue [the afflictions]?

Therefore, we know that the Mahāyāna is for the purpose of transcending the fruits. Now, let us explain this: when we speak of 'companions,' we mean merely those who provide indirect assistance; it does not necessarily require a state of association (saṃprayoga). This is why..."
The path with outflows (*sāsrava-mārga*) merely suppresses the companions of solitary greed (*rāga*) and so forth;

therefore, it is said that "companions" means they assist one another. Regarding the statement, "As for those who require association, because they reach the point of harming their companions," the intent is to challenge the previous master.

If one were to say that when I see the companions of views (*dṛṣṭi*), they must necessarily be associated with greed and so forth, and that there are no solitary companions such as greed, then how could there be [such companions] in the five stages?

It is stated that the "inferior companions" (*hīna-anucara*) associated with the eye belong to five stages (*pañca-bhūmika*). This clearly shows that it is admitted that there are independent (*svatantra*) greed (*rāga*) and so forth acting as companions to the view of self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).
It is not the case that [independent greed] is not permitted for those stages; rather, it is because independent greed and so forth serve as companions to the view of self.
To address this objection,
[Vasubandhu] says: "It does not state that 'the greed associated with it has already been subdued' means that even when manifesting solitary greed and so forth,
the worldly path is able to subdue them, which is what is meant by 'already subdued.'"
The Secret Master says: "This treatise states this explicitly; therefore, one who does not intentionally contravene it intends the following:

If one were to say that the name 'abandonment' refers to the afflictions such as the view of self within the sixth consciousness of the desire realm, then it would follow that one could give rise to higher [realms] while simultaneously abandoning lower delusions.

Since the treatise states that there is no giving rise to higher [realms] while abandoning lower delusions, it is clear that when the fruit arises, the person on the Path of Seeing gives rise to the view of self and so forth."
Yet [the opponent] maintains that one who has attained the third fruit is born in the higher realms.

[The Master] says in secret: "Nor can it be said that because they have not yet abandoned [the afflictions], or because of inversion, they are not obstructed. The intention is that this point is therefore broken again.
The external party offers a defense, saying: "Just as an Anāgāmin, although born in the higher realms, still [possesses] within the seventh manas-vijñāna either..."
Co-arising [defilements] do not obstruct the fruit and thus need not be abandoned; among the sixth category of defilements, those that can co-arise and do obstruct the fruit must be abandoned.
The *Mishū* (Secret Commentary) states: "Furthermore, regarding the discussion in the treatise that uses 'self' as a qualification, one should consult the text of that treatise."
The Secret [Commentary] says: "Those who composed the *Sāṃkhya* treatise" means that the Sāṃkhya non-Buddhists previously composed a *Sāṃkhya* treatise but did not provide an extensive explanation;
it is only now, within the *Saptati-śāstra*, that a full exposition is finally given, and thus it is called "concise."

The *Biji* (Secret Commentary) states: "According to reality, the formation of the sense-faculties consists solely of the *tanmātras* (subtle elements). This means that, according to the masters of the *Śāstra*, there are two theories. The first says:
the five *tanmātras* form the five great elements (*mahābhūta*), and these five form the five sense-faculties; this is the theory of successive mutual formation. The second says:

the five *tanmātras* collectively form the great elements, and collectively form the five sense-faculties. Based on this, the cause of the five sense-faculties is exclusively the five *tanmātras*. Therefore...

It is said: "That which can produce the faculties is exclusively the five subtle elements (tanmātras). For this reason, the sixteen principles are subsumed solely within the category of transformation;
thus, the Great One (mahat) and the others do not constitute the 'other' [the primal cause], and cannot be called the Root."
The Master [Bhāvaviveka] says: "If one takes 'another person' as the example for the reason 'because it is nameless,' the meaning is this:

if one takes the three *guṇas* (qualities) as the reason (*hetu*) and another person as the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), there is nothing established in the preceding [thesis]. This is because the thesis (*pakṣa*) is a conceptual construct while the example consists of real entities;

thus, the [reason] does not apply to the example, which is called 'the unestablished nature of the probandum' (*sādhyāsiddha*). If, however, one takes the three *guṇas* as the reason and an army or a forest..."
The concordant example (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta) constitutes the fault of lacking the probans (asādhana). The reason (*hetu*) is real, whereas the example is merely conventional;
thus, the reason does not apply to the example, and consequently, the example lacks the capacity to establish [the thesis]. This is the fault of lacking the probans.
The Secret Commentary (*Bimi*) states: "Regarding 'those such as the great elements (*mahābhūta*)... up to 'the same applies here,' the intent is as follows:

For instance, just as the great elements can constitute matter (*rūpa*), and matter is an object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is clearly known that the great elements and so forth are likewise objects of direct perception. Thus, when the sense faculties and so forth apprehend matter, they also apprehend the great elements, because the great elements constitute matter.
Since matter is already established as an object of direct perception, it is clearly known that the great elements and so forth [are also objects of direct perception]."

This is also obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Now, when I am established as being perceived by the sense faculties such as the eye, since that is already a matter of direct perception, it is clearly understood that the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*) is likewise obtained through direct perception. Therefore, it is said: "It should also be known according to this."

The Secret [Commentary] says: "To designate that which is subject to arising and ceasing as 'permanent' means that both [positions] rely on the fact that it does not perish or disintegrate to call it permanent;
fundamentally, this calculation is still [an instance of] impermanence through transformation."

The Secret [Master] said: "As for your school’s eighth category, the 'Moon'—if this is the fault you point out—it means that although the essence of the eighth is one, it does not preclude its transformation into distinct states such as mountains or non-mountains;
why should this be problematic for our school? How could the three virtues (triguṇa), whose essence is all-pervading and eternal, be obstructed by the many differentiated phenomena they produce?"
Biji said: "As for the statement that there are three pairs and six measures (*pramāṇa*), the intention is this:

this master divides this section of the commentary into three pairs in total, establishing six measures in order to refute the doctrines of other schools. If one follows this explanation, the underlying principles are not fully exhausted."
The Master of Secrets said: "His youthful appearance is beautiful. His intention was to say: "This Brahmin’s childhood name was 'Child-Scholar' (Kumārabhūta).
How could he not still be called 'Child-Scholar' when he is now grown? Here too, there are people whose childhood name was 'Little One' (Xiǎo);
how could they not still be called 'Little One' when they reach old age? Thus we know that although this Brahmin is somewhat advanced in years, it does not hinder [his status].
He is also called "Māṇava" (The Youth).
[Vasubandhu] says: "From 'perceiving pleasure' up to 'naming it the mind'—the meaning of 'mind' is this:
if I can cause the nine faculties not to be combined yet still be able to give rise to cognition, that is what is called 'I. Now, this mind causes the nine faculties not to be combined, and..."
The wise call this "intention" (*manas*). Question: Regarding the statement that they are "not in harmony," does this mean they are entirely not in harmony, or are they also in harmony?
Answer: It is not that they are not in harmony because of the Path; rather, they are entirely not in harmony.

Although this intention also possesses the nine virtues in harmony, it is not like the other [self], which possesses the nine virtues in harmony and thus has superior function. Therefore, it is said to be "not in harmony. In reality, however, it is also...
"Though they are combined, they do not overcome [the object].
Mi said: "That form relies on a single reality and is thus called 'relying on one' (ekāśraya). The meaning is this: "single reality" refers to a single ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*).
Even so, when the eye perceives based on a single ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), it requires the convergence of at least a maximum number of atoms before they can constitute an object.
This is because the objective field of form exists by having the ultimate atoms as its cause.
The Secret [Commentary] states: "Now, when it is said that the substance of the object depends upon a single reality (*ekadravya*), the intended meaning is as follows:

because the substance of the object is composed of many atoms (*paramāṇu*), it is therefore said that color-form (*rūpa*) depends upon a single reality. It does not mean that the eye can apprehend it by depending on a single color-form;

rather, the intended meaning is that it requires the aggregation of many atoms before the eye can obtain the object of color-form. It is not obtained by the eye depending upon a single atomic particle of color."

Although it is said that [the object] is not manifold and that the eye alone can apprehend it based on form (*rūpa*), this is stated with the intention of addressing the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

It does not mean that the eye can apprehend based on a single atom (*paramāṇu*) of form. The passage from "The treatise says, below" up to "is not called direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is intended to provide scriptural evidence.
Its meaning is as follows: for instance, if form were to depend upon a single atom, the resulting cognition would in all cases not be direct perception.
Regarding the measure: just as it is with the objective field of visible form (*rūpa*), so it is with odor and the other [objects].
The Secret [Master] says: "Alternatively, this is based on the fact that its substance is what is apprehended by the eye. The intended meaning is this: the atom (*paramāṇu*) is form;
for form to constitute a substance, it must be composed of multiple atoms. Therefore, when the eye perceives form, it also perceives a single, real atom. This is the basis upon which he speaks.

Regarding the principle that one obtains a minute particle (*paramāṇu*), in reality it cannot be obtained. Because this principle is subtle, it is not within the scope of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Mimi said: "It is not that the eye is permitted to grasp a single minute particle; rather, it is said that only when many minute particles are combined can they be apprehended."

The Master [Sthiramati] says: "The jar depends on its parts" means that, for instance, a minute measure (*aṇu-pramāṇa*) and a short measure (*hrasva-pramāṇa*) are both established upon two atoms (*dvyaṇuka*);

whereas a long measure (*dīrgha-pramāṇa*) and a large measure (*mahat-pramāṇa*) are established upon three atoms (*tryaṇuka*). Now, when two atoms are contrasted with three atoms, the short and long are designated as "minute" (*aṇu*) in relation to the "large" (*mahat*);

likewise, the large is designated as "minute" in relation to the [larger]. This is why it is said that "the jar depends [on its parts]. The term "depends" (*pratītya*) does not mean [that the jar is a mere conceptual construct].

When a subtle atom (*paramāṇu*) faces another subtle atom, it is said that their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are mutually dependent; the same applies to three subtle atoms, because they face one another.

The Master Mi says: "To say they are 'identical' by virtue of their mutual conformity" means that although these phenomena occur sequentially, they may still be called identical due to their conformity, just as smoke and fire exist both simultaneously and at different times.
The Secret Master said: "As for the statement that 'reaching [the object] is called seeing it as identical,' this master's intention is to say that one must see cause and effect as simultaneous;
therefore, it is called 'identical.'"
The Secret [Commentary] says: "To see the ripening grain is called 'seeing the same' (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa). As for the fault of non-pervasiveness, the meaning is as follows:
just as seeing fine grain seedlings allows one to know the seed, so too when seeing a fine seed, seeing the fine grain may also be called 'seeing the same.'"
When one sees the grain, does one also see the seed that is the cause capable of producing it?

Since one does not see it, it is clear that one cannot claim "seeing the same" on the basis of cause and effect being simultaneous. As for the fault of non-pervasiveness: if one says that smoke and fire are cause and effect...
Because they must necessarily exist simultaneously, it is called "simultaneous perception. To say that this is therefore "perception of sameness" entails the fault of non-pervasiveness. Why?

Because when one perceives a fine crop, although the manifest effect indicates a fine cause, one does not perceive that cause. Thus, it is clear that cause and effect are not identical in all respects;
hence, there is the fault of non-pervasiveness.

The Secret [Commentary] says: "Because their perceptions differ, those who have attained the arising of all-encompassing wisdom... The intended meaning is this: All causes and effects are mutually connected and unified in a single principle.

Yet, people perceive them as contradictory, just like those causes and effects. Although they are unified in a single principle—namely, the present union of cause and effect—the aspect of that union ultimately does not manifest;

therefore, it is said that it "ultimately does not manifest. As for "perceiving the object": *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "As for 'perceiving the object' (見境者). This phrase typically introduces a further explanation regarding how the practitioner perceives the objective realm within the context of meditative realization.*

The school maintains that cause and effect are harmonious and correspond to objects that can be directly perceived. However, due to the impairment caused by adverse conditions (*vipakṣa*), these objects ultimately do not appear.
If this cognition arises, it is termed inferential knowledge (*anumāna-jñāna*).
This is analogous, for example, to the way rain damages crops in the world.
The Master said: "Regarding the phrase 'the cause for reaching [the state] through conditions that are free from defilement,' the intended meaning is as follows:

'conditions free from defilement' refers precisely to the causes for the joy and exultation of right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). This exultation belongs to wisdom (*jñāna*). Question: What is meant by "conditions free from defilement"? Answer:

In this world, there are intelligent people who honor and draw near to virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) while distancing themselves from evil associates. Because they possess a sense of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), they cultivate the True Dharma. They practice...

At the time of this dharma, one is able to give rise to right knowledge in the future and thereby experience joyful exultation; thus, being free from the conditions of defilement, it serves as the cause for right knowledge.
The Master Bi says: "This 'negation' (*pratiṣedha*) refers to [the fact that] when [a cognition] reaches [an object] such as a quality (*guṇa*), it is able to take it as its object.

The meaning is this: because of this distinction, it is negated that the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) take qualities and so forth as their objects; rather, it is indicated that the mind and mental factors do take real entities (*dravya*) and so forth as their objects.

If this phrase expressing the distinction were absent, then at the time of cognizing a single dharma, one would have to cognize all dharmas. Question: Why does [the text] not first negate the cognition of real entities? And...

Does one first negate the qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth that serve as conditions? The answer is: Qualities do not exist independently; they must depend upon substances (*dravya*) as their substratum, while qualities themselves are the superstrata.
Therefore, one first negates the qualities and does not negate the substances and so forth. Since the substance is the fundamental basis, it is impossible to negate the substance first.

The Secret [Commentary] says: "To negate the causes of that cognition" means to negate the conditions such as qualities and recollection; "to indicate the causes of this cognition" means to indicate the real dharmas such as these conditions.

The Secret [Commentary] says: "As for 'possessing both parts' (ubhayāṃśika)," the intended meaning is as follows: that which is expressed consists of substance, quality, and action; because each possesses its own distinct essence, it is called "possessing both parts.
"Essence" (tattva) refers to the distinct categories, and "parts" (aṃśa) refers to the sense of being distinct classes. "Parts" thus carries the meaning of distinct categories.

The Master Mi said: "That which is called 'total difference' refers to the two categories of substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*). These two categories are also mutually termed 'total difference' when viewed in relation to one another.

The Master Mi said: "As for 'total sameness,' although there are nine substances, they are collectively subsumed into a single category of substance; this is called 'total sameness. [The same applies to] qualities..."
Karma is also to be understood according to this principle.

Regarding the term "differentiation within sameness" (*bhedasāmānya*), the intended meaning is as follows: for instance, when there is a single real atom (*paramāṇu*) of earth, although there are many atoms of earth [within it], they are collectively designated as "earth";
this is called "differentiation within sameness. While the individual substances of the atoms are many and thus differentiated, they are all equally "earth."
Therefore, they are called "identical.
As for [Master] Mi’s statement, "Each distinct meaning is called 'differentiation,'" this refers to the nature of multiple ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*).

As for Mi’s statement, "It resides within form; the same applies to the eye-faculty apprehending other faculties," the intended meaning is that because of the difference [in their respective objects],...
For this reason, it is perceived by the eye alone, because it is distinct from sound; the ear-organ perceives it accordingly, and the other organs follow this same principle.

As for the statement that "there is a distinct *ubhayabhāga* (part belonging to both)" regarding the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), the intended meaning is that the nine real entities (*dravya*) themselves are called *ubhayabhāga*.
Therefore, it is called the "general characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). It does not state that the substance of emptiness and so forth is manifold; thus, both name and benefit are divided.

The same applies to virtues and activities. Regarding the statement, "All realities harmonize within one reality," the intended meaning is that there are no real delusions in each and every stage (*bhūmi*).
All such [entities] consist of numerous atoms (*paramāṇu*). Although they are of many kinds, they are collectively designated as a single "real entity" (*dravya-pada*).
Therefore, all real entities are in conjunction; that which is one with respect to the real entity is precisely the "total aggregate" (*samudāya-bhāga*).
The Secret [Commentary] says: Regarding the meaning of "the single principle, its distinctions, and their shared aspects," the intent is as follows:

by virtue of the principle of a single reality, it is able to harmonize the various dharmas such as earth and so forth; by virtue of the principle of qualities (*guṇa*), it is able to harmonize form (*rūpa*) and cause the eyes and other faculties to perceive form and so forth;
and by virtue of the principle of action (*karman*), it is able to cause the appropriation of objects and so forth.
The Secret [Commentary] says: "When karma and so forth combine, there is a real basis. This means that in discussing combination, it must depend upon causes before the combination occurs.
When the Tathāgata combines with space, he requires seeds and the like for grain to sprout before he can combine with space.
This is like saying that when karma and so forth combine, there is a real basis, just as rain and grain stand in relation to one another.
It is also a conjunction of karma. Since this grain is composed of the atoms (paramāṇu) of earth and other elements, there exists a real substratum even before they have conjoined.
Therefore, it is said that at the time of the conjunction of karma and so forth, there is a real substratum. Regarding "separation is called impermanence":

because conditions are invariably separated from the real, separation is impermanent. Thus, what is impermanent is precisely the meaning of separation. How could there be a separation that is not [of this nature]?
"Is it eternal?
Mi replied, "Because they serve as homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the coarse levels (*audārika-bhūmi*), they are all impermanent.

This means that from the level of the subtle atom (*paramāṇu*) upward, these are designated as the coarse levels and so forth; since they act as homogeneous causes and are thus impermanent, it is clearly understood that upon these coarse levels and so forth—
Form, odor, taste, and touch are likewise impermanent.
[The Master] Mi said: "Subtle form" refers to the ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the parents; the intended meaning is that the resultant atoms arise from the ultimate atoms of the parents.
That is to say, the atoms of the parents' matter and the atoms of the child [act as] similar causes (*sabhāga-hetu*), because they are both matter.

Regarding the statement, "The gate of cause (*hetu-mukha*) is so named because it clarifies qualities (*guṇa*) by way of causes," the intended meaning is that within that treatise, the category of qualities is clarified according to the principle of causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
That is, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) combine to act as the cause and produce the quality of fragrance; how could this not be due to the primary elements?
[The opponent asks: "Is it because of this that the excellence of fragrance is clarified?
[Vasumitra] replies: "Regarding the two great atoms and the atom produced from them—the meaning is that the two great parent atoms are able to produce the atom that possesses fragrance;
this is precisely what constitutes the atom of fragrance. [The opponent] asks: "According to that calculation, fragrance exists only in the earth element (*pṛthivī*). How can this be reconciled?"

If it is said that from the two great atoms (*mahāparamāṇu*) a fragrance atom (*gandhaparamāṇu*) arises, and that this fragrance atom exists upon the great atoms, does this not contradict their [the Vaiśeṣika] tenet?

Answer: Although fragrance exists in the earth (*pṛthivī*), it does not arise dependent on the great atoms; thus, the quality of fragrance (*gandhaguṇa*) would not be concordant [with its substratum].

According to their explicit teaching, even if one were to grant that the fragrance atom depends on the great atoms, it would still obstruct [the claim that it] exists in the earth. Although such an interpretation exists, it is logically incorrect; therefore, it is said:

All of these contradict that treatise. Alternatively, this [interpretation] may be understood as "good," for it attains a transcendent formulation. If one relies upon this, the two meanings do not conflict.

As for the statement, "From the thirteen qualities beginning with *bodhi* up to the thirteen natures," the intended meaning is: although there are thirteen virtues such as *bodhi*, they have not yet reached the stage of being the thirteen natures.
Their essence is impermanent because they are not established based on reality. As for the thirteen similar categories that are explained together:
since the essences of these thirteen qualities are likewise all impermanent, they are somewhat similar. Because they are taught in a single location, it is said they are "explained together."

However, the four [qualities] such as fragrance and color are distinguished based on the real dharmas (dravyadharma) such as earth. If the atoms (paramāṇu) of the "parent" earth and so forth possess fragrance, they are impermanent;
as the commentary states, they are impermanent. If [fragrance] exists upon the "child" atoms, it is likewise impermanent;
the fragrances and other qualities that depend upon them are also impermanent.

The Master Mi said: "These ten categories, beginning with form (*rūpa*), differ according to their respective natures as being either permanent or impermanent, and as being gross atoms (*paramāṇu*) or subtle particles (*aṇu*).
Regarding these ten categories: earth possesses four qualities, namely the four beginning with form and fragrance; water possesses three, excluding fragrance."
Fire has two [characteristics], excluding taste; wind has one, which is touch alone.
Thus, there are ten types. The Secret Teaching says: "That which is solid is also called 'great' and 'subtle. The meaning is that it grasps the great and is also hard;
because it does not flow, it cannot possess the nature of liquidity."
The Master Bi said: "Speaking in terms of principle, that which is ultimately able to serve as a support for what is permanent means that visible form relies upon the atoms of fire;
therefore, it attains permanence. It does not rely upon the atoms of the earth element or those of the parents; therefore, it is impermanent. Question:

"If it does not rely [on them], how is it that you previously stated that what is apprehended by the eye is 'one support called form'? Answer: "This was said with reference to other [elements], such as water and fire."
Second is the theory of the parents' atoms (*paramāṇu*). It is not based on the theory of earth. [The Master] says in secret:

"That which is not eternally non-existent is called 'impermanent' (*anitya*). The intended meaning is: This is a statement made regarding non-existence; how can it be called impermanent? Because it is not [simply] non-existent.

If a phenomenon exists at some time and is then called "non-existent," then that very transition from existence to non-existence is what we call "impermanence. To say it is "non-existent" is merely a way of expressing this transition from existence to non-existence for the sake of brevity.
Therefore, that which is non-existent and impermanent does not exist; that which is eternally non-existent is itself permanent. Thus, it is said:

"The horns of a rabbit" are also included within the category of "non-existence" among the modes of expression. Are they, then, impermanent? Answer: The term "non-existence" (or "nothingness") has many applications.

When one says "non-existence" to mean that something is not expressed, this refers to that which is not eternally non-existent. As for that which is said to be eternally non-existent, it is not so described [in this context].
Therefore, it is said that while the general meaning is the same, the specific intentions differ.

[The Master] Mi says: "There is an interpretation according to which the object of the sense of hearing (*śrotra-āyatana*) and the object of the sense of touch (*kāya-āyatana*) are also present objects (*pratyakṣa-viṣaya*). The intention of this is as follows: according to this school of thought, the proponents of the "existence of objects" (*sākāra-vāda*), [the objects of these two senses are indeed perceived].
The objection states: "Earth and the other elements are form (*rūpa*). When the eye perceives form, it also perceives earth and space.

Since it also perceives that which serves as the basis for sound, when the ear perceives sound, it likewise perceives space. As these two principles are identical, by what means can the objection be refuted?

Now, to explain the intent of the secret response: Earth and the others are objects of vision; thus, when the eye perceives form, it also perceives earth and space. However, their essence is not an object of hearing; therefore, the ear [does not perceive them].
Because when sound is perceived, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is not heard, it is said that the manifestation of emptiness and so forth is constant.
The Master Mi says: "If [an object] depends upon the Great [Elements] and is not a single real entity, it is called a manifest object. The intended meaning is this:

if one were to say it depends upon a single real atom (*paramāṇu*), it could not be called a manifest object; however, if it depends upon coarse matter (*sthūla-rūpa*), it can indeed be called a manifest object.
"Large" means not being a single atom (*paramāṇu*). That which is "large" is not small;
that which is "not a single atom" is because it consists of many atoms.
The Secret [Commentary] says: "As for the phrase 'only being able to create the cause and not creating the difference,' the meaning is this:

although I am able to create the cause, I do not create the fruit; I merely receive the fruit created by the earth. Question: Since one is already able to create the cause, how could one not be able to induce the fruit? Answer:

This is explained in terms of directly receiving the fruit, not in terms of creating the cause. Once the cause has been obtained and the fruit has been obtained, it is because of the creation of the cause [that the fruit arises].
"Attainment of the fruit [is possible], because it is separated by one layer. Bi said:

"According to those who explain based on the 'possessing' [category], the intention is as follows: among the ten phrases, four phrases are capable of producing the fruit—namely, substance, quality, action, and existence.
The remaining five phrases combined cannot produce it. However, there is no phrase for 'non-existence'; although there are 'permanent' and 'impermanent,' there is none [for non-existence]."

It does not produce a fruit; this is not what is being stated here, because it is distinct from non-existence (*avastu*). Thus, it is not negated. Subsequently, the ten qualities (*guṇa*) are able to produce a fruit.

As for the "ten qualities," they are: color (*rūpa*), taste (*rasa*), touch (*sparśa*), moisture (*drava*), number (*saṃkhyā*), distinctness (*pṛthaktva*), dimension (*parimāṇa*), cause (*kāraṇa*), heaviness (*gurutva*), and conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
Although these ten qualities are generally constant, they do produce a fruit.
Bimi said: "The five being direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) means that their qualities and activities coincide together; the five not being direct perception is likewise so. Bimi said:
"It is not necessary for them to be contrasted with one another to be called 'many' (*bahu*); it is simply a matter of number. That which is not one is called many.
It does not require a specific quantity; it is merely the appearance of multiple jars that is called 'many'."

The Secret [Commentary] states: "The six phrases can be understood" means that the six phrases, such as "reality" (satya) and so forth, are not subsumed within the ten phrases of the fundamental systems of the non-Buddhists;
therefore, it says they "can be understood. These six phrases subsume the ten phrases, as will be explained in detail below.

The Secret Commentary says: "There is an interpretation that [the categories] generally include the 'semblance' (sadr̥śa). Regarding the statement 'at the time of the subsequent explanation,' the intent is as follows:
if one asserts that many are substantially real, then the six [categories] are like dharmas of semblance—just as an army or a forest—and these are thus semblances.

If one relies on the former interpretation, where only the six phrases are said to be real, then provisional (prajñapti) dharmas would not be included. If one relies on the latter interpretation, then nine phrases are real, with the exception of the phrase 'inexpressible' (avaktavya)."

Therefore, it is called "mostly real" (*bāhulika-satya*), because it is mostly real rather than entirely real in its totality. Consequently, things such as armies and forests are also included therein;
this clearly shows that the latter explanation is superior. If one were to state only the first six phrases, then the six phrases concerning armies, forests, and so forth would not be subsumed.

The Secret [Commentary] says: "In order to preclude this, it does not say 'there is no agent. The intended meaning is that, in order to preclude indetermination, it takes 'the absence of activity' as the reason."
The Secret [Text] asks: "If it occurs again, why is it not obstructed? The intention of this question is as follows:

The answer is that if one takes the eternally abiding, non-arising fruit as the cause, then this very cause can also function as described above. This is because True Suchness (tathatā) is eternally abiding and does not arise as a fruit.
The second is the indeterminate interpretation. As there is a passage below, [the opponent] says:

"Is it not the case that when a *dharmin* (a subject possessing properties) establishes another *dharmin*, the eternally abiding [nature], which does not produce an effect, is itself a *dharmin* that is now being used as a reason (*hetu*)?
Since a *dharmin* is being used as the reason, does this not mean that a *dharmin* establishes a *dharmin*?"
Question: This is a case where a property-possessor (dharmin) establishes a property-possessor. Why do you say that a property-possessor establishes a property-possessor? Answer:

The essence of this reason (*hetu*) is precisely the aforementioned property-possessor; because it transforms the former property-possessor into the present reason, it is said that "a property-possessor establishes [another] property-possessor.
This is stated with reference to its original state, for the essence of the reason was originally a property-possessor.
Mi says: "Because there is nothing upon which it depends. This means that since the preceding *dharma* is taken as the cause, the cause has nothing upon which it depends.
Mi says: "Question: To what extent does this other-inference (*parārthānumāna*) avoid being 'inconclusive' (*anaikāntika*)? The intention is this:

even if one were to grant that our eternal *dharmas* do not produce effects, they would not be like a rabbit's horn, which does not produce an effect; therefore, [the reason] is excluded [from being inconclusive].

Does consciousness have an intrinsic nature? This is to say that you admit it does. Is it like [the case of] conjunction and disjunction, where qualities do not produce difference, such that there is an intrinsic nature apart from consciousness?
This points out the fallacy of the "undetermined" (*anaikāntika*). Question: Does this fallacy of the undetermined hold? Answer: It does not hold. Why?

Because, in discussing the fallacy of the undetermined, both parties must agree upon the instance. Now, since the Mahāyāna does not admit [the existence of] conjunction, disjunction, and so forth, [the instance is not shared].
"How can it be established as an inconclusive fallacy (*anaikāntika*) if there exists something distinct from conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*)?
He replied: "It is like the case of Chu and Yue. This means that the administrative principles and laws of the two states of Chu and Yue were distinct;

likewise, in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya-ṭīkā*, the logical principles of the three types of inference (*trividha-anumāna*) are differentiated and analyzed, just as Chu and Yue are distinct. Thus, the three types of inference...

That which is called "inference for oneself" (*svārthānumāna*), "inference for others" (*parārthānumāna*), and "common inference" (*sādhāraṇānumāna*). The masters of *hetuvidyā* (logic) distinguish these three types of inference with extreme clarity.
Why, then, do you now ask: "Is this not an inference for others? How can it not be the fallacy of 'inconclusiveness' (*anaikāntika*)?"

The Secret Commentary (*Bimi*) states: "As for this treatise being 'still thus' (*zhi you er zhe*), the intended meaning is as follows: For instance, in the case of the *Yinming shu* (Commentary on Logic), the analytical dissection is extremely clear;

however, if one encounters this treatise and finds it often muddled and confused, then even though one establishes autonomous inference (*svabhāvānumāna*) based on its own level, it is not clear in common [usage], and is therefore certainly muddled and confused.
The phrase "sweet herbs and mugwort still intermingle" is intended to explain the meaning of "muddled and confused. However...
Regarding the twenty types of mugwort that resemble ginseng: those who do not recognize them mistakenly conceive of the sweet mugwort as being ginseng. Question:

If a Mahāyāna Dharma Master is thoroughly proficient in Vijñaptimātratā (Consciousness-Only) and possesses a clear understanding of both *svārthānumāna* (inference for oneself) and *parārthānumāna* (inference for others), like a bright pearl, why is it that in this treatise, the meaning and the text often appear to be disconnected?
Answer: It is not that he lacks mastery himself; rather, he is demonstrating a particular perspective (*digdarśana*). There is... [text fragment].
Regarding its second intention: first, it is to test whether those who study have attained realization or not.
That the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* contains this intention means that throughout the *Abhidharmakośa*, Master Vasubandhu frequently expresses this; as the text says: "I do not say... [and so forth].
"This is merely to test those scholars.
Mi said: "The two remaining masters of *hetuvidyā* (logic) arrived, so he showed them their errors. The meaning is that he was referring to those masters of *hetuvidyā*.

Regarding the fault of [relying on] a single cause, he does not differentiate the nine cases. Now, the Mahāyāna Dharma Master likewise follows the words of the aforementioned Hetuvidyā master, which is why he does not differentiate them.
Furthermore, because he wishes to generate awakened wisdom, he demonstrates fallacious arguments.
A "fallacious argument" (prasanga) refers to that which is deficient in expression and erroneous in principle.

The Master Bi said: "Now, regarding the 'dissimilar example' (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta), the intended meaning is as follows: since both [the subject and the example] are permanent, whereas cognition and so forth are impermanent, it is therefore a dissimilar example.
Thus it is said: 'The example differs from the example; cognition, etc., are equal.'"

The Secret Commentary states: "Regarding 'the thesis and the reason being identical or different,' the intended meaning is as follows: the thesis statement implies that [the object] should not be separate from consciousness;

since cognition and so forth are indeed not separate from consciousness, cognition and so forth constitute the similar class (*sapakṣa*) in terms of their verbal designation. As for 'the reason being different,' this intends to show that cognition and so forth serve as the dissimilar example (*vipakṣa*) within the same category."

The Secret [Commentary] says: Regarding the nine propositions of the "gate of categories," that which is also the "correct cause" (saddhetu) intends to clarify that the proposition should be the eighth;
that is, it is both existent and non-existent, and different from "also non-existent. Question:

Since even a partial transformation can serve as a cause, how is it established that sound is a property-possessor (dharmin) and is necessarily impermanent? The reason (hetu) is stated as: "because it is produced by volitional effort."

Because it is of the nature of that which is produced. This is illustrated by the analogy of a jar. Now, when it is said that [the probans] exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), this refers to the jar as being of the same class as the cause;

thus it is said that it "exists" in the similar class. As for the statement that it does not exist [in the similar class], this refers to a flash of lightning, which is not a similar instance of the cause; therefore, it is said that it "does not exist.
Although one part of the jar belongs to the similar class of the cause, one part of the lightning does not belong to the similar class of the cause. This is because...
This is a similar instance (sapakṣa) to the thesis; therefore, it is said to function as a valid reason (*saddhetu*). Now, the reason for "eternality" is likewise so:
although it exists in relation to pleasure and consciousness, and even upon a rabbit's horn, because these are similar instances to the thesis, they also serve as valid reasons.

This is just like the reason of "uninterrupted effort," which, although absent from lightning, serves as a valid reason because it is a similar instance to the thesis. Thus, it is said that the similar instance is one.

Regarding "partial pervasion" (*ekadeśavṛtti*): if one takes a jar as the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), because the jar possesses the quality of being produced immediately following volitional effort, it can serve as the class of the reason (*hetu*).
However, because lightning is produced immediately following volitional effort, it cannot be taken as the similar instance. Therefore, partial pervasion is also a valid correct reason (*saddhetu*).
Even though a jar and lightning are of the same kind in relation to the thesis (*pakṣa*), when viewed from the perspective of the reason, they differ.

One part functions, while one part does not. Although the lightning does not function upon the upper part, it nonetheless serves as a correct cause (*saddhetu*). The eternally abiding cause (*nityahetu*) is likewise:
although it is absent from [the locus of] cognition and so forth, it is nevertheless asserted to be a correct cause for the existence of rabbit horns.
The Secret Master says: "That which is 'unequaled' is also merely a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) of the thesis, because that which is 'unequaled' is not separate from consciousness.

The Secret Master says: That treatise states, "It fully clarifies that which can produce a fruit. The intended meaning is this: although awakening (*bodha*) serves as the cause, it nevertheless produces the fruit.

Regarding the statement, "Whether as a single entity or a distinct entity, that awakening serves as the cause," it means that precisely because that awakening serves as the cause, the [resultant] portion arises.

[They are] distinct. Regarding the phenomena of identical essence and distinct essences: if there were no pervasion (*āpūraṇa*) and so forth, one could not differentiate between phenomena of identical essence and multiple essences.
To say "this essence" and "that essence," taking distance and proximity as the cause, means that one takes the cognitions of nearness and farness as the cause.

It acts as the faculty of discernment. This essence, by virtue of its pervasive nature as a cause, discerns that very essence; that which is grasped by one's own sense faculties constitutes one's "own body.
The terms "this" and "that" are applied relative to one's own faculties, not in reference to another's body.

Miji says: "If one follows the topical outline (shuke) of the Commentary, as for the phrase 'reaching what is subsumed under their respective divisions,' the meaning is that according to the preceding outline in the Commentary, this single section of text concerning earth, water, and fire is not included."

The Secret [Commentary] states: "The body attains touch, up to the body attaining earth and so forth. The intended meaning is that touch depends upon earth and the other elements; that is to say, when the body attains touch, it also attains earth and the others.
It means that touch exists in dependence upon earth and the rest. If one attains the maintenance of touch, one likewise attains earth and the other elements.
The Secret [Commentary] says: "Regarding the mutual correspondence of sense-faculties and objects," the intended meaning is this: the body-faculty perceives only tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*).
Although the earth possesses visible form (*rūpa*), the body-faculty fundamentally does not perceive that form; for form is perceived only by the eye-faculty, and not by the body-faculty.
The Secret [Teaching] says: "It is not that one who has not attained all virtues such as the stages (bhūmi) [can attain it]. This means:
even by means of the path that lacks a supporting stage (anāśraya-bhūmi), one causes the body-faculty (kāyendriya) to attain [it]. Why? Because the faculty and its object do not face one another.

The Secret [Commentary] says: "That which [the opponent] calls 'earth' by virtue of both the semblance and the real" means that if, within the Buddha-dharma, solid phenomena are designated as earth and form (*rūpa*) is designated as the semblance of earth, whereas non-Buddhists designate the color seen by the eye as "jewel-earth"—then when it is said here that both the provisional and the real are called "earth," the various stages (*bhūmi*) are the provisional earth;
these, in relation to the "form" and "mirror-like nature" of other schools, are collectively termed "earth."
The Master Mi says: "Those who contradict this and that treatise" means that the ten-verse treatise of those externalists is precisely the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only).
The Master Mi says:

"If it were to incur even one of the faults attributed to others" means, according to the explanation in the Commentary (*Śū*), that within the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*), there is no difference between the substance and its qualities.

"Touch" (*spraṣṭavya*) refers to what is admitted by the Mahāyāna itself: because the "great" (*mahat*) within the [category of] substance (*dravya*) does not coincide with the "touch" within the category of quality (*guṇa*), one commits a fault corresponding to whichever [of these two] is transgressed.

Question: If all four great elements (*mahābhūta*) possess touch, why are earth and the others not mentioned? Why is it that while the "great" is not distinct from the touch among qualities, it is specifically stated that the "great" is not distinct from the touch among qualities [alone]?
Answer: Just as the other three great elements possess color (*rūpa*) and so forth—three, four, or one—and many [qualities], [the same applies here].
The minor [elements] are indeterminate; there are only the major [elements], which possess only two kinds, namely color (*rūpa*) and tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*).
This is why the major colors differ from the partial ones. Now, according to other schools, those schools do not admit that the "major" is identical to tangibility;
thus, according to their own tenets, there is no fault.

The Secret [Commentary] says: "Because the reason (*hetu*) is indeterminate (*anaikāntika*). The meaning is this: if one takes only a single attribute-phrase (*guṇapada*) as the thesis (*pakṣa*), it is not equivalent to the others;

thus, there is the fault of being indeterminate. As for that fault: does this attribute-phrase lack an essence (*svabhāva*) apart from consciousness—like the son of a barren woman—because it is not included among real things?
Or is it like "Great Existence" (*mahāsattā*) and so forth, which, though not included among real things, do possess an essence apart from existence?
Yes. [Master] Mi said: "The 'single category and single reason' refers to one category and one reason. Mi said:

"The intention behind establishing a separate one later is that the initial formal inference (*pramāṇa*) does not distinguish between a single entity and multiple entities; it generally establishes eight propositions (*aṣṭapada*)."
This constitutes one means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The subsequent [means], "non-existence of reality" and so forth, are explained by analogy with the first single entity-dharma.
Therefore, taking "non-existence" as the reason, it is established as a separate means of valid cognition; together they constitute two means of valid cognition, which refute the nine positions.

The *Biji* says: "It is not restricted; it is localized in 'neither real nor existent. The meaning is this: one does not take 'neither real nor existent' as the reason for an inference (*anumāna*), which would restrict it to those two locations.
Rather, within the nine propositions (*navapada*), it is obtained according to the method of formulation."

The Secret Commentary says: "Because it is permitted to be the co-existent root for other consciousnesses. This means that the eighth consciousness is permitted to serve as the co-existent root for other consciousnesses.

The Secret [Commentary] states: "Regarding the fault of 'a partial deviation from the object of qualification' (*viśeṣya-ekadeśa-aprasiddhi*), the intended meaning is as follows: 'the other' (*para*) refers to that which is called the Buddha-dharma;
that is, the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Furthermore, when the Buddhist doctrine (*buddhadharma*) is contrasted with them, it constitutes a deviation from a portion of the object of qualification."

The Secret Commentary states: "Because the reason also possesses the fault of being 'limited to one' (*ekāntika*) in relation to the other" means that when the non-Buddhists further employ an inference against the Buddha-dharma, their reason possesses the fault of being limited to one.
That is to say, because it is limited to one in relation to the other, it is called the fault of being "limited to one."

Regarding the passage "Mi says: 'There is a sense in which, when the principle of existence reaches the state of non-existence, it is then non-existent,'" the intended meaning is that this represents the general position of the proponents of existence (*astitvavādin*), recounting the salvific intent of the Vaiśeṣika masters.
Regarding the passage "Mi says: 'The commentary states... up to "one and eternal,"'" this is the interpretation of [the author of] the *Zhong* (the *Zhongguan lun*).

Mishu said: "One might say this is like a white jade disk that still bears a flaw. The meaning of this is that there is a reasoned defense of the terminology; the interpretation of the intent is quite excellent.

However, the expression is loose and deficient. In what way is it deficient? If one says that in our system causes and effects exist, and because they now arise and perish together, they do not depend on a coming into being from what already exists—then consider, for instance, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
It is also called the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*) and is also called the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*). Its function...
This is what you have said. [Yet] how can there be arising and ceasing within that which is unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) cause and effect? Such words are overly broad; thus, they are lax and deficient.
It may be said that even a flawless white jade disc still bears a blemish. Furthermore, although a white jade disc is a fine treasure, if it has even a slight flaw...

People do not find this beautiful or weighty. Now, if you attempt to rescue your own doctrine by asserting that cause and effect involve arising and ceasing, although the reasoning may be sound, there is ambiguity in your terminology.
This is because unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) causes and effects are neither arising nor ceasing; it is like a white jade disc that has a flaw or blemish.
"Jade" (*guī*) refers here to precious stone.

The Secret Master says: "If one were to raise a partial objection regarding permanence that fails to distinguish [between the two], the intent would be to reprimand the proponents of existence for failing to distinguish a single locus.

For if you say, 'Because my causes and effects are impermanent, they both possess arising and ceasing and do not depend on the coming and going of existence,' then since your causes and effects are permanent, they should likewise possess the coming and going of existence. Why, then, in your defensive text, do you fail to make this distinction?"
The Secret [Text] says: "If your 'realities' (*satya*) and other phenomena arise simultaneously," the meaning is:
if your realities and other phenomena arise only by having causes, then those realities and others must be neither unitary nor eternal. The intent is to say:

if realities and other phenomena depend upon causes to arise, then those realities and other phenomena must be neither unitary nor eternal; that is, emptiness and so forth are not unitary, and atoms (*paramāṇu*) are not eternal.
"It ought not to be eternal.
Mi said: "This refers to the Lord of Logic (Dignāga). Regarding the phrase 'it ought not to be truly a refuter,' the intended meaning is as follows:

In the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra*, the Bodhisattva Dignāga described the fault of the externalist's thesis being contradictory to its own specific characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*), and then stated: 'Your great existence ought not to be...'"

Regarding the nature of "great existence" (mahābhūta): the term "you" (bhavān) serves to exclude [the position of] one's own school. Thus, through inference, the proof and refutation are established as authentic, and there is no fault of contradiction with the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of the phenomenon.
Why, then, is it said that using the term "you" still entails the fault of contradicting one's own words?
This is explained in detail in the *Nyāyapraveśaka-ṭīkā*. As for the "Lord of Devas" (Devendra), he is the Bodhisattva Śaṅkara; this is his name, "Lord of Devas."
This is because it was obtained through the sacrifice to Heaven.
Mi said: "As for the statement that 'if an existent phenomenon (bhāva-dharma) is used to establish another existent phenomenon, various faults arise,' the intended meaning is:

if one takes an existent phenomenon and further uses it as an analogy, then that very phenomenon will result in various faults. Question: "If an existent phenomenon is taken as an analogy, then it is an existent phenomenon that establishes [the point]."

Question: How does the analogy relate to the fault of establishing an existent phenomenon (bhāva) by means of an existent phenomenon? Answer: Because the very phenomenon being discussed is used as the analogy, it is explained in terms of that original phenomenon.

Since the analogy is an existent phenomenon, it is provisionally designated as an existent phenomenon; thus, there is the fallacy of establishing an existent phenomenon by means of an existent phenomenon.

The Secret [Commentary] says: "It is not that one takes the aforementioned words as being truly of the nature of virtue and activity. The meaning is this: even if one employs them, these are not truly of the nature of virtue and activity;

thus, although they constitute a thesis within their respective phrases, they are not accepted. Furthermore, that which they grasp as being truly of the nature of virtue and activity is certainly not so according to the ultimate principle;
therefore, the text rejects it. Why is this asked and answered? It is because they merely reject it in general and do not treat it as a valid measure (*pramāṇa*).
