The Secret [Commentary] says: "There is an interpretation that this is also a general illustration for the thesis (*pakṣa*). As for the phrase 'conjoining the meaning of the sentence,' the intent is as follows: 'such as qualities (*guṇa*), activities (*karma*), etc.'—the term 'etc.

includes the general illustrations for the thesis. Question: What are these general illustrations for the thesis? Answer: They are precisely the three phrases beginning with "not the thesis" (*na pakṣa*).

That is to say, they are explained as having the sense of the "conjoined sentence" (*sāmagrī-vākya*). The "commonality and difference" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) is merely the subject (*dharmin*). In reality...

The "nature of equality" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) constitutes both the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*). The reason is so called because it differs from [the categories of] substance (*dravya*) and so forth, just like the term "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*).

If one takes the three terms—substance, quality (*guṇa*), and action (*karman*)—and turns them into the thesis and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), they are then termed a "distinct thesis" and a "distinct example," as explained in the Commentary.

If one uses "conjunction" as the example to generally refute both sameness and difference, rather than [refuting] the nature of substance and so forth, this is termed the "example for the general thesis."

The Secret [Commentary] says: "Regarding the establishment of the roots and objects," this means it is stated that the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) is not a rational object. It is clearly known that the category of "substance" (*dravya-pada*) is not entirely obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

As for the phrase "the entirety of these [three] phrases is divided into two [of the remaining]": the intention is that among the three phrases—namely, action (*karma*), existence (*bhāva*), and generality/particularity (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*)—the entirety is obtained through direct perception;

however, within the two phrases of substance and quality (*guṇa*), only a small portion is so obtained, while the remainder is not obtained through direct perception. One should examine the preceding [passages].
"The gate is not manifest; one knows the gate of the manifest object.
The Secret [Commentary] says: "How could it be that what precedes and follows devours one another? The intent is this: "Devouring" refers to large and small fish taking turns eating each other.

If one were to say, as the Master of the *Yìshū* (Commentary on Meaning) does, that among the meanings of the preceding gates, the five phrases constitute direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), how could this be?

"Could it be that what is now being stated—real existence, qualities, and so forth—is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? How could one possibly contradict oneself by asserting [these] in succession, like eating fish and meat?
Miyu replied: "When one says 'an existent phenomenon is called a phenomenon,' this refers to calling an existent phenomenon by its name; it is not the *pakṣadharma* (the property of the subject)."

The Master Bi said: "Regarding the statement that the word 'condition' (*pratyaya*) resides within the property (*dharma*), the intended meaning is this: it is difficult [to establish] this word 'condition' within the property.
If it were truly present among the properties, one would not have previously admitted the non-existence of cognition (*buddhi*) and so forth;

yet now, by placing the word 'condition' within the subject-property (*pakṣadharma*), how could it possibly exclude the fault of [the reason being] a property of the subject? Therefore, the inclusion of the word 'condition' merely excludes contradiction."
This is a flaw in your thesis. You cannot simply dismiss the objection by saying it "follows from the characteristics" (*xiàng cóng*).

If you grant that a single mind can simultaneously take two objects as its conditions, then those two objects following one another are designated as "a single object of cognition. It is impossible for a single mind to simultaneously take only one object;

it can only do so at the point where the two objects meet. Therefore, you say it "follows from the characteristics. Furthermore, regarding the term "placing the condition" (*zhì yuán*) used in reference to the aspect of non-separation, what purpose does it serve?
Jian Mi said: "By using the word 'only' (*kevala*) here to exclude this [attainment], the intention is as follows:

if the word 'only' were present, although it would exclude attainment through specific conditions (*pṛthak-pratyaya*), it would not exclude attainment through general conditions (*sāmānya-pratyaya*). This is because the word excludes attainment through general conditions; therefore, it is also not [the case that]..."
The character "wei" (唯) is used; it is determined solely according to the treatise. [The Master] Bi said:
"Regarding the statement that the *Mahābhāṣya* discusses Maheśvara up to the *Nirvāṇa-śāstra*, the intended meaning is as follows:

Bodhisattva Deva composed the *Nirvāṇa-śāstra*, in which he set forth the views of the non-Buddhists and the Hīnayāna. He asserted that a person creates nirvāṇa; thus, the name of the sūtra is 'Nirvāṇa'."
[The] *Pan* [treatise] states therein: "This was composed by the master of treatises Maheśvara.
Regarding those who speak thus of Mahādeva, he has three names: first, Brahmā; second, Nārāyaṇa; and third, Maheśvara. Question:
Now, it is said that he has three names: first, Brahmā; second, Nārāyaṇa; and third, Mahe...
Śiva asked: "If it is said that what has a cause must necessarily perish, how can its fruit be such that cause and fruit are called 'one who creates'?
Answer: We do not say that the creator of the cause cannot produce the fruit; rather, because the objects of expectation differ, we say that cause and fruit are each created separately."
Thus, they receive their names in relation to what precedes and follows them. When the bird is actually performing the causal action, it is called the fruit of Brahmā;
when it reaches maturity, it is called the creation of Nārāyaṇa.
The Secret [Text] says: "Earth is the locus of support; reaching earth is the body. This means that Maheśvara takes empty space as his head and the great earth as his body.
Question: Why was it previously stated that earth is the locus of support for Maheśvara, yet now it is said to be his body?
Answer: Once the body is understood through its basis of support, then earth is the locus of support for Maheśvara.
Regarding the term "abode" (sthāna): the underlying meaning is that it is said the earth is the body of Maheśvara.
[The Master] Mi said: "The Lord of Sovereignty (Īśvara) is the cause of arising and ceasing; the body of Rāhu is the cause of arising and ceasing. As for the Lord of Sovereignty:
This refers to Maheśvara. "Dwelling in the heavens of form" means dwelling in the Akaniṣṭha heaven (the Highest Heaven of Form).
Regarding the secret statement, "The Vedic masters [trace their lineage] back to the Progenitor," the intended meaning is that the Vedic masters are the masters of the Śāstras.
Those masters claim that the Progenitor was born from the center of Nārāyaṇa’s navel; furthermore, he created all living beings.
Because he is not on the side of conditioned beings (*sattva*), he is named the Patriarch (*pitāmaha*). Question:

Since Nārāyaṇa and Brahmā are one body with different names, how can there be a distinction between high and low, such that Brahmā is born from Nārāyaṇa? Answer: There is no fault in this. It is like the case of the *svasaṃbhogakāya* (self-enjoyment body).
The emanation body flows forth to teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to sever evil and cultivate goodness, so that they may attain birth in superior realms and the like.

Regarding the secret [teaching], it says: "Transforming into mountains and wilds" refers to those who attain birth in such places; the intended meaning is that even the birds and beasts within the mountains [are included].
...transformations, as well as pigs, sheep, and other such species among humans. If one harms or kills them to make offerings to Brahmā, one shall further attain rebirth in that realm.

[The Master] said in secret: "Regarding the phrase 'at the time,' it means 'perishing when the time arrives. The intention is to say that the so-called 'real interval' (tattva-antara) postulated by the non-Buddhists exists..."
"Prosperity is followed by decline; all is due to time.
Mi said: "As for what is called the *Prakṛti-ātmaka* teacher, he derived his name from that which he served.
*Ātmaka* (or *An-ta*) refers to *prakṛti* (the primal source). It is a substance of spiritual and supernatural nature, much like the characteristic of the *puruṣa* (the self)."

It is similar [to the aforementioned]. Because it is capable of creating all things. This means: at the beginningless time when the sun, moon, stars, space, earth, and so forth did not yet exist, there was at that time only fire and water.
